m1-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Pick the right Thonny installer for your computer and install it.
  • Open Thonny for the first time and find the editor and the Shell.
  • Type a line of Python in the Shell and read what comes back.
  • Fix the setup problems that stop most beginners.

Ask the calculator on your phone for 2 to the power of 100. Most will show something like 1.2676506e30, a rounded guess. Python gives you every one of the 31 digits: 1267650600228229401496703205376. Twenty minutes from now, your own computer will do that.

#What you're installing, and why Thonny

Python is a language, and the Python interpreter is the program that reads Python code and carries it out. You also need an editor, a place to type code and save it. Thonny packs both into one download: install Thonny and you have Python.

There are many Python editors. This course uses Thonny because it was designed at the University of Tartu for people writing their first programs. Two of its features matter a lot later: a Variables panel that lists every value your program is holding, and a debugger that runs your program one step at a time so you can watch it think. Thonny is free and open source, with no account to make.

You need:

  • A Windows 10 or 11 PC, a Mac with macOS Catalina (10.15) or newer, or a Chromebook that allows Linux apps.
  • About 15 minutes (closer to 30 on a Chromebook, because switching on Linux takes a while).
  • No administrator password on Windows or a Chromebook. A Mac will ask for the password you log in with.

📝 Note

Already installed Python from python.org? Keep it. Thonny uses its own private copy of Python, so the two don't get in each other's way.

#Install it, step by step

Windows

  1. Find out what kind of processor your PC has. Open Settings › System › About and look at System type. Most PCs say x64-based processor. Some newer laptops with Snapdragon chips say ARM-based processor.
  2. Go to thonny.org. In the download box at the top, under Windows, click Installer with Python 3.14 for Intel or AMD computers (a file named like thonny-5.0.1-x64.exe). If your PC is ARM-based, pick the installer for Arm instead. If the version number on the site is newer than 5.0.1, take the newer one.
  3. Open the downloaded file from your Downloads folder.
  4. If a blue box says Windows protected your PC, click More info, then Run anyway. Windows shows this for programs it hasn't seen installed very often; it is not a virus warning.
  5. If you're asked how to install, choose Install for me only. This puts Thonny in your own user folder, which is why no administrator password is needed.
  6. Click Next past the license (it's already accepted for you) and the suggested folder. Tick Create desktop icon if you want one. Click Install, and when the last page says Great success!, click Finish.
  7. Open Thonny: press the Windows key, type Thonny, and press Enter.

macOS

  1. Open the Apple menu (top left) and choose About This Mac. If you see Chip followed by Apple M1, M2, M3, M4 or similar, you have an Apple silicon Mac. If you see Processor with Intel in the name, you have an Intel Mac.
  2. Go to thonny.org. Under Mac, click Installer with Python 3.14 for Apple Silicon Macs (a file named like thonny-5.0.1-arm64.pkg) or the one for Intel Macs (thonny-5.0.1-x64.pkg). If the site shows a newer version, take it.
  3. Open the .pkg file from Downloads. Click Continue, agree to the license, and click Install. Type your Mac login password when asked.
  4. When it says the installation was successful, click Close. If it offers to move the installer to the Trash, that's fine; you won't need it again.
  5. Open Thonny from your Applications folder or from Launchpad. If macOS checks that you really want to open an app downloaded from the internet, click Open.
  6. The first time you save into Documents or Desktop, macOS may ask whether Thonny can use that folder. Click Allow, or Thonny won't be able to save there.

Chromebook

Thonny runs inside the Chromebook's Linux environment, which is switched off until you turn it on.

  1. Click the time in the bottom-right corner, then Settings. Go to About ChromeOS › Developers. Next to Linux development environment, click Set up and follow the prompts. Setup can take 10 minutes or more. When it finishes, a Terminal window opens.
  2. In the Terminal, type the first line below and press Enter. When it finishes, type the second line and press Enter. The first refreshes the list of available software, and the second installs Thonny.
  1. Open the launcher (the circle in the bottom-left corner) and look in the Linux apps folder for Thonny.

This installs the copy of Thonny packaged for Linux, which can be a version or two behind the Windows and Mac downloads. Every lesson in this course works with it.

If Developers or Linux development environment is missing, the Chromebook is probably managed by a school that has switched Linux off. See the fixes at the bottom of this page.

#Open Thonny for the first time

The very first launch shows a small window titled Welcome to Thonny! with two menus. Leave Language on English (or pick yours), leave Initial settings on Standard, and click Let's go! The other choice, Raspberry Pi (simple), hides the menu bar, and this course uses the menus.

The main window has two parts you'll use every day:

  • The editor, the big area at the top, with a tab labeled <untitled>. This is where you'll write programs and save them as files.
  • The Shell, the area underneath. It starts with a line that begins Python 3. followed by a version number, and then a >>> prompt. The Shell runs a single line of Python the moment you press Enter.

Across the top is a row of buttons: New, Load, Save, a green Run button, a Debug button with a bug on it, the step buttons Over, Into, and Out, a Resume button, and a red Stop sign. You'll meet the ones that matter over the next few lessons.

#Prove it works

Click just to the right of >>> in the Shell. Type each line below and press Enter after each one:

Your Shell should now look like this:

print(...) displays whatever is inside the brackets. ** means "to the power of", so 2 ** 100 is 2 multiplied by itself 100 times. The Shell also shows the value of any calculation you type, even without print, which makes it a handy calculator. Programs saved in files don't do that, so the next lesson uses print for everything.

If you got those three answers, Python and Thonny are installed and working. If you got red text instead, the next section covers the usual causes.

💡 Tip

Text too small? Use View › Increase font size (Ctrl and + on Windows and Chromebook, Cmd and + on a Mac). Bigger text means fewer typos.

#When setup goes wrong

#Windows says "This app can't run on your PC"

The installer doesn't match your processor. Check System type again (step 1) and download the other Windows installer.

#The installer is blocked and there's no Run anyway button

School and library computers often block installers. Ask whoever runs the computer, or try Thonny's portable variant: on thonny.org, under Windows, download the .zip labeled Portable variant. Right-click it, choose Extract All, put the folder in your Documents, then open the folder and double-click thonny.exe. Nothing gets installed, so it often works where installers don't.

#The Shell shows red text or never shows >>>

The hidden Python process that Thonny talks to didn't start properly. Click the red Stop button (or choose Run › Stop/Restart backend, Ctrl+F2). That restarts Python and usually brings the prompt back. If it keeps happening, close Thonny and open it again.

#On a Mac, Thonny can't save files or says "Operation not permitted"

You probably clicked Don't Allow when macOS asked about folder access. Open System Settings › Privacy & Security, find the section for files and folders, and switch on access for Thonny. Then quit Thonny and open it again.

#The Chromebook has no Linux option

Schools can turn Linux off on managed Chromebooks, and only their administrator can turn it back on. Ask your teacher or school tech team. Until then, Python Tutor (pythontutor.com) runs short Python programs in the browser and shows variables step by step, much like Thonny does. It's enough to follow along with the first few modules while you sort out a computer that can run Thonny, such as a home or public-library PC.

Key takeaways

  • Thonny's installer includes Python, so one download sets up both.
  • The editor (top) is for programs you save; the Shell (bottom) runs one line at a time.
  • 2 ** 100 printing all 31 digits proves your setup works.
  • The red Stop button restarts Python when the Shell gets stuck.

#Further reading

  • Thonny's home page (opens in a new tab): the download box, plus a short list of features with screenshots of the debugger.
  • Thonny's FAQ (opens in a new tab): answers from the developers about installation problems and unusual setups.
  • Set up Linux on your Chromebook (opens in a new tab): Google's own steps for switching Linux on, and what to do if it misbehaves.

m1-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Tell the editor and the Shell apart, and know when to use each.
  • Make a course folder and save a program in it as a .py file.
  • Run a program and match each line of output to the line of code that made it.
  • Break a program on purpose and read the error message Python gives back.

Anything you type in the Shell disappears when you close Thonny. That's fine for a quick sum, but real programs need to be kept, changed, and run again tomorrow. So programs live in files, and Python files end in .py.

By the end of this page you'll have a file called first_run.py that works out how many times your heart beats in a day, saved somewhere you can find it again.

#Editor or Shell?

Both run Python, but they do different jobs:

Use the Shell to test a tiny idea ("what does 7 / 2 give?"). Use the editor for anything you'd want to run twice.

#Step 1: Make a folder for this course

Every program you write in this course will go in one folder. Make it now, outside Thonny:

Windows

Open File Explorer and click Documents on the left. Right-click an empty spot, choose New › Folder, and name it beginner-python.

macOS

Open Finder and click Documents in the sidebar. Choose File › New Folder and name it beginner-python.

Chromebook

Open the Files app and click Linux files on the left. (Thonny can only see files in this area.) Right-click an empty spot, choose New folder, and name it beginner-python.

Use exactly that name: lowercase, with a dash instead of a space. The next lesson explains why spaces in names cause trouble.

#Step 2: Type the program

Click in Thonny's editor (the <untitled> tab) and type these four lines. Type them yourself rather than copying: your fingers learn where the brackets and quotes go.

Each line is one instruction. Inside each print(...), the part in quotes is text that gets shown exactly as typed. The part after the comma is a calculation; Python works it out first and then prints the answer. The comma tells print to show both things with a space between them.

#Step 3: Save it as first_run.py

Press Ctrl+S (Cmd+S on a Mac), or click the Save button. In the dialog, open Documents, then your beginner-python folder (on a Chromebook, it's in your home folder), type first_run.py as the name, and click Save.

The editor tab now says first_run.py instead of <untitled>. If you forget the .py, Thonny adds it for you.

#Step 4: Run it

Click the green Run button, press F5, or choose Run › Run current script. On a Mac, F5 may need the fn key held down; Cmd+R works too.

Look at the Shell. Thonny writes %Run first_run.py to show which file it ran, then the program's output appears underneath, matching the output shown above.

Match each output line to its code line. Line 2 printed 86400, never 60 * 60 * 24, because Python works out calculations before printing them. Only the text inside quotes is printed exactly as written.

🧪 Try it yourself

Change 70 to your own resting heart rate (most teens are somewhere between 60 and 100), then click Run again. Thonny saves the file for you every time you run it, so you don't need to press Save first.

#Step 5: Watch it run one line at a time

Python runs a file from the top line to the bottom line, one line at a time, and never skips ahead. Step through the same program below and watch the output grow by one line per step.

Thonny can do the same thing with your file. Click the Debug button (the bug) or press Ctrl+F5. The first line is highlighted, and nothing has run yet. Now press F6 (the Over button) to run one line. Keep pressing it and watch the Shell fill up.

Want to go even slower? Press F7 (the Into button) instead, and Thonny shows a calculation like 60 * 60 * 24 being worked out piece by piece: first 3600, then 86400. You'll use this a lot from Module 2 onward. Note that Thonny can only debug a program that has been saved.

#Step 6: Break it on purpose

Every programmer sees error messages every day. The skill is reading them calmly. Make each change below to first_run.py, run it, read the error, then undo the change.

Break 1: delete the closing quote on line 1.

Python reads the opening " and keeps looking for the matching one until the line ends. The last line of the message names the problem: an unterminated string literal, meaning text that was opened and never closed. The line number above it tells you where. Thonny also underlines the problem spot in the editor.

Break 2: change print to Print on line 1.

Python is case-sensitive, so Print and print are different names, and nothing called Print exists. This is a NameError, and Python even suggests the fix: Did you mean: 'print'?

Break 3: delete the last ) on line 2.

Every ( needs a matching ). Notice that this error stopped the program before line 1 ran, so nothing was printed at all. Python checks the whole file for this kind of mistake (a syntax error) before it runs anything.

When a program crashes, Thonny may open an Assistant panel on the right with a plain-English explanation. Read it, but read Python's last line first: that's the one you'll see in every editor, for the rest of your programming life.

#Proof that your setup works

Tick these off before moving on:

  1. first_run.py is in your beginner-python folder. Check in File Explorer, Finder, or Files.
  2. Close Thonny completely, open it again, and use File › Open (or File › Recent files) to open first_run.py.
  3. Click Run. You get the same four lines of output, with no red text.

If all three work, your computer is ready for the rest of the course.

Check your understanding

2 questions

1You type print(60 * 60) in the editor, save, and run. What appears in the Shell?

  • The calculation isn't in quotes, so Python works it out instead of printing it as text.

  • Python evaluates 60 * 60 first, then prints the result.

  • Files don't show bare calculations, but print always displays what it's given.

Show answer

B. Python evaluates 60 * 60 first, then prints the result.

2A program's line 2 is missing a ). Line 1 is a correct print. What happens when you run it?

  • That's how most errors behave, but a missing bracket is a syntax error, found before anything runs.

  • Python checks the whole file's grammar first, so line 1 never gets a chance to run.

  • Python never guesses what you meant; it stops and tells you.

Show answer

B. Python checks the whole file's grammar first, so line 1 never gets a chance to run.

Key takeaways

  • Programs live in .py files; the Shell is for quick one-line tests.
  • Python runs a file from top to bottom, one line at a time.
  • The last line of an error message names the problem, and the line number tells you where to look.
  • Debug (Ctrl+F5) plus Over (F6) lets you run your program one line at a time.

#Further reading

  • Python's official tutorial: using Python as a calculator (opens in a new tab): more Shell experiments with numbers and text, from the people who make Python.
  • Python Tutor (opens in a new tab): paste a short program and step through it in your browser, a good second view of what Thonny's debugger shows.

m1-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Use each kind of lesson in this course (Notes, Build-along, Practice) the way it was designed.
  • Organize your programs in module folders with names Python can handle.
  • Read a Python error message in four steps, starting from the last line.
  • Follow a routine for getting unstuck, and stop a program that won't stop.

Here's a bug that catches someone in every beginner class. You write a dice game, save it as random.py because it uses random numbers, and run it:

The code is fine. The file name is the bug. import random is supposed to load Python's built-in random-number tools, but Python looks in your folder first, finds your own random.py, and loads that instead. Your file has no randint in it, so the program crashes. Rename the file dice_game.py and it works. (Python versions older than 3.13, like the one some Chromebooks install, give a vaguer message about a "partially initialized module" for the same mistake.)

This page is about habits like that: small things that save hours.

#How the lessons in this course fit together

Modules 2 to 7 each teach one big idea in three lessons:

Lesson What it is How to use it
1: Notes The ideas, with small examples you can run Read with Thonny open. Retype the examples and change them.
2: Build-along One complete program, built a step at a time Build it yourself in your own file, running it after every step.
3: Practice Six exercises that get harder, plus a challenge Try each one before you open the hint, and the hint before the solution.

Module 8 is a capstone: you plan and build a program of your own choosing.

Three habits make the biggest difference. Type the code rather than pasting it; that's how you learn where the colons and brackets go. Predict before you run: say out loud what you think a program will print, then check. Being wrong and finding out why is where most of the learning happens. And when a lesson offers a step-through animation, actually step through it, because it shows the thing beginners can't see: values changing.

#One folder, one subfolder per module

You made beginner-python in the last lesson. Inside it, make one folder per module, and save each program in the folder for the module it belongs to:

Move first_run.py into m1 now. When you're looking for "that program with the bike prices" a month from now, you'll know where it is.

#Name files so Python can use them

Python file names follow the same rules as names inside Python, and breaking them causes problems later, when you try to import one file from another.

  • Use only lowercase letters, digits, and underscores, and end with .py: bike_fare.py, exercise_3.py.
  • No spaces. my program.py runs today but can't be imported tomorrow.
  • Don't start with a digit. 3_exercise.py has the same import problem.
  • Never name a file after something Python already has: random.py, math.py, time.py, string.py, turtle.py. Thonny pops up a Potential problem warning if you try some of these. Take the hint.

💡 Tip

Before you make a big change to a program that works, keep a copy. File › Save as… with a new name like bike_fare_v2.py means you can always go back to the version that worked.

#Save often, and know where your files really are

Thonny saves your file every time you click Run, but only after it has a name. An <untitled> tab is lost if Thonny crashes, so give every program a name before you write more than a couple of lines.

On a Chromebook, the Linux files area lives only on that Chromebook. It isn't copied to Google Drive, and removing Linux deletes it. After each module, copy your beginner-python folder into Google Drive in the Files app. On Windows and Mac, if your Documents folder syncs to OneDrive or iCloud, you're already covered.

#Read an error message from the bottom up

An error message is called a traceback. It looks scary because it's long, but it's always built the same way. Here's a program with a typo on its last line:

Read it in this order:

  1. The last line first. It gives the error's type (NameError) and a message in plain-ish English: there's no variable called games_payed. Python even guesses what you meant.
  2. The line number. File "main.py", line 5 tells you which line crashed. (In Thonny you'll see your own file name; click it to jump to that line.)
  3. The carets. The ^^^^ marks under the code point at the exact part that failed.
  4. The line itself, and the one above it. Here the fix is on line 5: payed should be played. For syntax errors, the real mistake is often at the end of the line above the one Python reports.

Notice that line 4 ran and printed before the crash. Python runs lines in order, and it stops at the first line it can't run. Everything above that line already happened.

#A routine for when you're stuck

Being stuck is a normal part of programming, not a sign you're bad at it. What matters is having a next step. Work through this list in order:

Two of these need explaining. Explaining out loud works surprisingly often: when you say "this line adds the tax… wait, no it doesn't", you find the bug yourself. Programmers call this rubber-duck debugging, after the idea of explaining your code to a rubber duck on your desk.

Asking well gets you help faster. Include the code, the whole error message, what you expected to happen, and what you've already tried. "It doesn't work" can't be answered; "line 5 gives NameError and I expected it to print 0.7" can.

If you use an AI chatbot, ask it to explain the error message rather than to rewrite your program. You'll learn to fix it, and next time you won't need to ask.

#When a program won't stop

Sometimes a program seems frozen. Usually it's one of two things:

  • It's waiting for you to type something. A program that uses input() pauses until you type an answer in the Shell and press Enter. Click in the Shell and look for a prompt.
  • It's stuck repeating forever. You'll meet loops in Module 5, and one that never ends will keep printing or keep the Shell busy.

Either way, the red Stop button (or Run › Stop/Restart backend, Ctrl+F2) ends the program and gives you a fresh >>> prompt. Nothing is lost: your file is still in the editor.

Key takeaways

  • Never name a program after a Python module like random or math; Python will load your file instead.
  • Keep one folder per module, and use lowercase names with underscores.
  • Read errors from the bottom: the type and message, then the line number, then the carets.
  • When stuck: read, step through, explain out loud, search, and then ask with code, error, and expectation.
  • The red Stop button rescues a program that's waiting or looping forever.

#Further reading

  • Errors and Exceptions in the Python tutorial (opens in a new tab): the difference between syntax errors and the errors that happen while a program runs.
  • Built-in Exceptions (opens in a new tab): look up any error type you meet, like NameError or TypeError, and see exactly what it means.

m2-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Create a variable and update it, reading = as "becomes".
  • Predict what a program prints by tracking each variable line by line.
  • Tell the four basic types apart: str, int, float, and bool.
  • Watch variables change in Thonny's Variables panel and debugger.
  • Spot the silent bug a typo in a variable name causes.

A welcome kiosk in a library lobby greets each visitor by name. Read this program and decide, before you look at the output, whether it welcomes Ana or Ben:

It welcomes Ana, even though visitor is "Ben" by the time print(greeting) runs. Line 2 built the text "Welcome back, Ana!" at the moment it ran and stored that finished text. Changing visitor on line 3 doesn't go back and rebuild it. A variable isn't a formula that keeps itself up to date, like a spreadsheet cell; it holds whatever value was last put in it.

That one idea explains most of the surprises beginners meet with variables, so the rest of this page builds on it.

#A variable is a name stuck on a value

Here's the intuition: a value like "Ana" or 15 sits in the computer's memory, and a variable is a name tag stuck onto it so you can find it again. Moving the tag to a new value doesn't change the old value; it just means the name now points somewhere else.

Now precisely. A line like visits = visits + 1 is an assignment, and Python always handles it in two steps:

  1. Work out the right-hand side, using the values the variables have right now.
  2. Make the name on the left refer to the result.

So the = sign doesn't mean "is equal to" the way it does in math. Read it as becomes: "visits becomes visits plus one".

On line 3, Python reads visits (it's 1), adds 1 to get 2, and only then makes visits refer to 2. Line 5 uses +=, a shortcut that means exactly the same thing as visits = visits + 1. You'll see += everywhere in real code, along with -= for subtracting.

#Watch the values change

Step through a slightly longer kiosk program. Keep your eye on the variables list: each assignment adds a name or changes one value, and print never changes anything.

When you reach the last line, three things should make sense. visits is 2 because it was increased twice. first_visit is False because the later assignment replaced True. And greeting still mentions Ana, because it was built before visitor changed.

#Order matters: Python can't look ahead

Python runs your file from top to bottom and only knows about a variable once the line that creates it has run. Use a name too early and the program stops:

NameError: name 'name' is not defined means "I've never heard of this name". The variable is created on line 2, but line 1 runs first. The fix is to swap the two lines. Whenever you see a NameError, ask two questions: is the name spelled the same everywhere, and does the line that creates it run before the line that uses it?

#Every value has a type

Python sorts values into types, and the type decides what operations do. You'll use four constantly:

Type What it holds Examples
str (string) Text, always inside quotes "Ana", "15", ""
int (integer) Whole numbers 0, 15, -3
float Numbers with a decimal point 4.5, 0.25, 15.0
bool (Boolean) One of two values: True or False True, False

The built-in type() function tells you the type of any value. Watch how the same symbol does different jobs depending on the types around it:

3 + 4 adds numbers and gives 7, but "3" + "4" glues two pieces of text together and gives 34. And "15" is a str, not an int, because the quotes make it text that happens to look like a number. That difference causes one of the most common bugs in Module 3, when your programs start reading what people type.

True and False are written with capital letters and no quotes. A bool answers a yes-or-no question, like whether this is someone's first visit. Module 4 uses them to make decisions.

#Watching variables in Thonny

You don't have to track values in your head. In Thonny, open View › Variables. A panel appears that lists every variable your program has made, with its current value.

  1. Open kiosk_greeting.py (or type it in and save it in your m2 folder).
  2. Click Run. The Variables panel now shows the final value of each name.
  3. Now click Debug (Ctrl+F5) and press F6 (Over) one line at a time. Watch greeting appear in the panel with Ana's name in it, and then watch visitor change to "Ben" while greeting stays exactly the same.

This is the single most useful debugging habit you can build. When a program prints something you didn't expect, step through it and find the first line where a value in the panel isn't what you thought it would be. The bug is on or just above that line.

#Choosing names Python accepts (and humans understand)

Python is strict about the shape of a name:

Name Allowed? Why
first_visit Yes Letters and underscores are fine
visitor2 Yes Digits are fine after the first character
2nd_visitor No A name can't start with a digit
first visit No No spaces; Python sees two names
Visitor Yes, but… It's a different name from visitor, because case matters
print Technically, but don't It replaces the real print for the rest of the program

Try one of the forbidden ones and you get a syntax error before anything runs:

Beyond the rules, pick names that say what the value means. visits beats v, and first_visit beats flag. Python programmers write multi-word names in lowercase joined by underscores, a style called snake_case.

⚠️ Watch out

A typo makes a brand-new variable, with no error. This program is meant to add 5 points:

It prints 10. Line 2 created a second variable called scroe and stored 15 in it, while score stayed at 10. Python can't know you misspelled it. The Variables panel gives it away, because you'd see both score and scroe listed. Whenever a value refuses to change, look for a twin with a slightly different spelling.

⚠️ Watch out

Quotes turn a name into plain text. print("visitor") prints the word visitor. print(visitor) looks up the variable and prints its value, like Ben.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A program runs price = 4, then total = price * 3, then price = 5, then print(total). What does it print?

  • total was worked out as 4 × 3 when its line ran. Changing price afterwards doesn't redo that calculation.

  • That would only happen if total updated itself like a spreadsheet formula. It doesn't; it keeps the value it was given.

  • There are no quotes, so Python calculates the expression instead of printing it as text.

Show answer

A. total was worked out as 4 × 3 when its line ran. Changing price afterwards doesn't redo that calculation.

2After count = 7 and then count += 2, what is count?

  • += changes the variable: it adds 2 to the current value and stores the result back.

  • count += 2 means count = count + 2, so 7 + 2 = 9 is stored in count.

  • That would happen with text ("7" + "2"), but 7 and 2 are integers.

Show answer

B. count += 2 means count = count + 2, so 7 + 2 = 9 is stored in count.

3Which value is a str, not a number?

  • The decimal point makes this a float, a number.

  • The quotes make it text. It looks like a number, but Python treats it as two characters.

  • A minus sign doesn't change the type; this is an int.

Show answer

B. The quotes make it text. It looks like a number, but Python treats it as two characters.

4A program sets lives = 3, later has the line livs = lives - 1, and finally prints lives. What do you see?

  • Assigning to a name creates it, so livs = … makes a new variable without complaint.

  • The typo stored 2 in a new variable, livs, and lives never changed.

  • That would be right if the name were spelled lives on both sides of the =.

Show answer

B. The typo stored 2 in a new variable, livs, and lives never changed.

Key takeaways

  • = means "becomes": Python works out the right side first, then stores it under the name on the left.
  • A variable keeps the value it was given; it doesn't update when other variables change later.
  • Python runs top to bottom, so a variable must be created before it's used, or you get a NameError.
  • str, int, float, and bool are the four basic types, and "15" is text, not a number.
  • View › Variables plus stepping with F6 shows every value as it changes, which is the fastest way to find a bug.

What you'll learn

  • Plan which values a program needs to remember, and pick a type for each.
  • Update variables with +=, -=, and a calculation.
  • Print a status line that shows the current state after each change.
  • Use Thonny's debugger and Variables panel to find a bug that causes no error message.

Games are a good place to practice variables, because a game is mostly a pile of values that keep changing: health goes down, gold goes up, a door unlocks. You'll write a four-scene adventure called The Lantern Cave. The story is fixed (you'll make it respond to the player in later modules), but every number in it is tracked and updated by the program.

Here's the plan, with what each scene does to the hero's stats:

Make a new file in Thonny and save it as adventure_stats.py in your m2 folder. Open View › Variables too, so you can watch the values as you go.

📝 Note

Each step below adds lines to the bottom of your file. The output under each step shows only what the new lines print. In Thonny, clicking Run runs the whole file, so you'll see the earlier output above it as well.

#Step 1: Decide what to remember

Before writing any story, list the facts about the hero that can change, and choose a type for each:

Variable Type Starting value Why this type
hero str "Robin" A name is text
health int 100 Health points are whole numbers
gold int 0 You can't have half a coin
bag_kg float 1.5 Weight needs a decimal point
has_key bool False You either have the key or you don't

Type the setup, plus a title and a first status line:

The first line starts with #, which makes it a comment: a note for humans that Python skips. The long print mixes text in quotes with variable names without quotes, separated by commas. Python prints each piece with a space between them, swapping each name for its current value.

Run it and check the Variables panel. You should see all five names with their starting values.

#Step 2: The forest

The hero finds 40 gold and picks up a lantern weighing 0.75 kg. Add a blank line, a line of story, the two updates, and a fresh status line:

An empty print() prints a blank line, which spaces the scenes out. gold += 40 reads the current gold (0), adds 40, and stores 40. bag_kg += 0.75 does the same with a float, so the bag now weighs 2.25 kg.

Notice the order: story first, then the updates, then the status. If you printed the status before the updates, it would show the old values, because print shows what's stored at the moment it runs.

#Step 3: The river

-= subtracts: health goes from 100 to 70. You've now typed the same status line three times. That's a sign that something could be packaged up and reused, and later in the course you'll learn to do exactly that with a function. For now, copying it is fine.

#Step 4: The market

The potion's price goes in its own variable, so the story line and the subtraction can't disagree about what it costs:

If you later decide potions cost 15, you change one number and both the message and the math follow. Typing 12 in two places would work today, but sooner or later someone changes one and forgets the other.

#Step 5: The cave, and a bug with no error message

Bandits take half the hero's gold, and the hero finds a brass key weighing 0.25 kg. Here is the scene as a beginner might first type it. Add it and run it:

The story says the bandits took half the gold, but the status still says 28. There's no red text and no crash, so the error message routine from Module 1 can't help. This is the kind of bug the debugger is for.

Click Debug (Ctrl+F5) and press F6 repeatedly until you reach the bandits line, keeping your eyes on the Variables panel. After that line runs, a new name appears in the list, glod, holding 14, while gold sits unchanged at 28. The typo created a second variable instead of updating the first. You can step through the same moment here:

Fix the spelling so the line updates gold itself:

Now the gold drops to 14. Why // and not /? Both divide, but / always produces a float, so you'd get 14.0 coins. // divides and throws away anything after the decimal point, which keeps gold a whole number. Module 4 covers both properly. In your file, delete the old glod line rather than adding this fix underneath it.

#Step 6: The ending

Finish with a score that combines two stats. Each coin is worth 10 points, and every point of health left counts once:

Python multiplies before it adds, just like in math class, so this is 14 * 10 + 90, which is 230.

#The finished program

Here is the whole file in one piece, with the bug fixed. Run yours and compare.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why is has_key stored as False rather than as the text "no"?

  • It can; any text works as a string. The question is which type fits the meaning.

  • True and False can't be misspelled as "No" or "nope", and Module 4's decisions can use them directly.

  • The difference is too tiny to matter. The reason is meaning and safety, not speed.

Show answer

B. True and False can't be misspelled as "No" or "nope", and Module 4's decisions can use them directly.

2In Step 5, what would gold = gold / 2 have stored?

  • That's what // gives. Plain / always produces a float.

  • / always returns a float, even when the division comes out even, so the status would show 14.0 gold.

  • Dividing an int is fine; the result is just a float.

Show answer

B. / always returns a float, even when the division comes out even, so the status would show 14.0 gold.

3The status line was printed after the updates in every scene. What would printing it before the updates show?

  • print shows what is stored at the moment it runs, and the updates haven't happened yet.

  • Python never looks ahead; it runs one line at a time, top to bottom.

  • Reading a variable before changing it is completely normal.

Show answer

A. print shows what is stored at the moment it runs, and the updates haven't happened yet.

Key takeaways

  • Start a program by listing the values that will change, with a sensible type for each.
  • += and -= update a variable using its current value.
  • Put a value used in more than one place, like a price, in its own variable.
  • A misspelled name creates a new variable with no error; the Variables panel shows the twin.
  • / always gives a float, while // drops the decimal part.

#Make it yours

  • Add a fifth scene between the market and the cave, with its own change to two of the stats.
  • Track a new value, such as torch_minutes, that goes down in every scene.
  • Change the score formula so each kilogram in the bag costs 5 points. Work out the new score on paper first, then run it to check.
  • Introduce a bug of your own (a typo, or a -= that should be +=), give the file to a friend, and see how fast they find it with the Variables panel.

#Further reading

  • Python Tutor (opens in a new tab): paste the finished program in to see every variable drawn as a box as the story runs.
  • Numbers in the official tutorial (opens in a new tab): more on /, //, and mixing whole numbers with decimals.

What you'll learn

  • Predict a program's output by tracking every variable on paper.
  • Fix NameError crashes caused by order and spelling.
  • Swap the values of two variables without losing either one.
  • Use Thonny's Variables panel to find the line where a value goes wrong.
  • Recalculate a value that depends on other variables each time they change.

Make a file for each exercise in your m2 folder (ex1.py, ex2.py, and so on), and keep View › Variables open while you work. Try each exercise before opening the hint, and try the hint before opening the solution.

Warm-up. In the Shell, type n = 4, then n *= 3, then n. Before you press Enter on the last one, say what you expect. *= multiplies a variable in place, the same way += adds.

#Exercise 1: Predict it on paper

Without running it, work out exactly what this prints:

Write your answer down, then run it to check.

Need a hint?

Draw a table with a column for laps and a column for best, and one row per line. On each line, only the variable on the left of = changes. Line 2 copies the value laps has at that moment.

Show solution
Line laps best
laps = 2 2
best = laps 2 2
laps = laps * 3 6 2
best = best + laps 6 8
laps -= 1 5 8

Line 2 copies the number 2 into best; it doesn't tie best to laps. That's why tripling laps on line 3 leaves best at 2.

#Exercise 2: Fix the ticket printer

This program should print a two-line ticket, but it crashes. Fix it so the output is exactly:

Need a hint?

There are two separate bugs. Fix the one the error points at, run it again, and let the next error lead you to the second. One is about order, one is about spelling.

Show solution

The first NameError happens because guest is used on line 1 but not created until line 2, so the print moves below the assignment. The second is the typo seet. Fixing errors one at a time, rerunning after each, is normal: Python only ever reports the first problem it hits.

#Exercise 3: Swap two items

A game character holds a sword in the left hand and a shield in the right:

Add lines so that print(left, right) prints shield sword. Here's the first idea most people try. Step through it and watch the sword disappear:

Need a hint?

After left = right, nothing refers to "sword" any more. Before you overwrite left, put its value somewhere safe: a third variable.

Show solution

spare keeps the sword while left gets overwritten, and then right takes it from spare. Python also has a one-line swap, left, right = right, left, which works out both values on the right before assigning either. It's worth knowing, but make sure you understand the three-line version first, because most other languages need it.

#Exercise 4: Savings jar

Start a variable jar at 0 and print it after each week:

  • Week 1: you save 12.50.
  • Week 2: you save 12.50 again.
  • Week 3: you spend 8.75 on a game.
  • Week 4: you save 12.50 and get 20 for your birthday.

Sample output:

Need a hint?

Use += for money in and -= for money out, with a print after each week. Python drops the trailing zero in 12.50; Module 3 shows how to always print two decimal places.

Show solution

jar starts as the int 0 and becomes a float the moment a decimal is added. In week 4, Python works out 12.50 + 20 first and then adds that 32.5 to the jar.

#Exercise 5: The practice log that undercounts

This program should add up three days of guitar practice, but it reports 90 minutes instead of 135. Don't read it line by line looking for the bug. Instead, save it, click Debug, press F6 line by line, and find the first line after which total in the Variables panel isn't what it should be.

Need a hint?

After line 4, total should be 45. After line 5, it should be 45 + 30. What is it really?

Show solution

Line 5 replaced the running total with Tuesday's minutes instead of adding to it, so Monday's 45 was thrown away. In the debugger, total drops from 45 to 30 at that line, which is the clue. Writing total += tuesday would also work.

#Exercise 6: Quiz-bowl scoreboard

Two teams, the Owls and the Foxes, start at 0. A correct answer is worth 10 points and a wrong buzz loses 5. Here's what happens:

  1. Owls answer correctly.
  2. Foxes answer correctly.
  3. Foxes buzz in wrong.
  4. Owls answer correctly.
  5. Foxes answer correctly.

After each question, print both scores and the Owls' lead (Owls minus Foxes). Sample output:

Need a hint?

It's tempting to write lead = owls - foxes once at the top. Remember the kiosk greeting from the Notes: a variable doesn't update itself when the values it was built from change. Where does the line need to go?

Show solution

lead is recalculated after every score change. If you calculated it once at the top, it would be stuck at 0 for the whole game. A value that is worked out from other variables has to be worked out again whenever they change.

#Challenge: Musical chairs

Three friends sit in seats A, B and C:

Everyone moves one seat along: whoever was in A moves to B, B moves to C, and C wraps around to A. Write the moves so that print(seat_a, seat_b, seat_c) prints Lu Jo Kai. Use only one spare variable. Then find a way to do it in one line.

Need a hint?

Every move overwrites someone, so start by putting one person in the spare variable. If you save the person in C first, which seat can you fill straight away without losing anyone?

Show solution

Saving Lu first frees up seat C, so Kai can move in, which frees seat B for Jo, and finally Lu comes out of spare into seat A. Each move fills the seat that the previous move just emptied. In the one-line version, Python reads all three values on the right before changing any of them, so nobody gets overwritten.

m3-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Pick out characters and pieces of a string with indexes and slices.
  • Clean and change text with string methods, and keep the result.
  • Turn typed answers into numbers with int() and float(), and read a ValueError.
  • Format output with f-strings: decimal places, column widths, and alignment.
  • Ask yes-or-no questions about text with in, .isdigit(), and .startswith().

A club sign-up program gives 2 free stickers with every T-shirt. Someone orders 3 shirts:

Thirty-three stickers. No error, no warning, just a wrong answer that a real person would see. The cause is the most important fact on this page: input() always gives you text, even when the person types digits. "3" * 2 repeats the text twice, giving "33". By the end of this page you'll know how to fix it, and why it happened.

#A string is a row of characters

Text in Python is a string (str): a sequence of characters in a fixed order. Each character has a numbered position called an index. Counting starts at 0, and negative numbers count back from the end:

Square brackets pick out characters. Put a colon inside them to take a slice, a piece of the string from one index up to, but not including, another:

len() counts the characters: 8. club[0:4] takes indexes 0, 1, 2 and 3, and stops before 4, giving Robo. Leave out a number and the slice runs to that end of the string, so club[4:] is everything from index 4 on. The "up to but not including" rule seems odd at first, but it means club[:4] + club[4:] always rebuilds the whole word.

Ask for an index that doesn't exist and Python stops:

The last index of an 8-character string is 7, because counting started at 0.

#String methods clean and change text

A method is a function that belongs to a value. You call it with a dot: club.upper(). Strings have dozens of methods, and a handful do most of the work in programs that read what people type:

The square brackets are printed only so you can see where the spaces are. .strip() removes spaces from both ends, but leaves the spaces in the middle alone. .title() capitalizes the first letter of each word and lowercases the rest, and .lower() and .upper() change everything. You can chain methods, as in raw.strip().title(): Python runs them left to right, each on the result of the one before.

Here is the rule that causes the most bugs: strings never change. Every method gives back a new string and leaves the original as it was. So this does nothing useful:

The stripped copy was made and immediately thrown away. To keep it, store it: name = name.strip().

#Yes-or-no questions about text

Some string tools answer with True or False instead of a new string. They're the bridge to Module 4, where your program will act on the answer:

in checks whether one piece of text appears inside another, and it's case-sensitive, so "Bot" isn't found. .isdigit() is True only when every character is a digit, which is why the decimal point makes "20.5" fail. Lowering a reply before checking it means Yes, yes, and YES are all treated alike.

#Numbers: converting between text and numbers

Back to the stickers. To do math with what someone typed, convert it first. Each type's name works as a converter:

You have You want Use Example Result
"3" a whole number int() int("3") 3
"2.5" a decimal float() float("2.5") 2.5
3.99 a whole number int() int(3.99) 3 (it chops, it doesn't round)
7 / 3 2 decimal places round() round(7 / 3, 2) 2.33
15 text str() str(15) + "!" "15!"

Step through the fixed sticker program and watch the type of each variable. shirts holds the text '3', while count holds the number 3:

Most programs convert straight away, in one line: shirts = int(input("How many club T-shirts? ")). Python runs the inner part first (show the question, wait for the answer), then hands the text to int().

int() is forgiving about spaces around the digits (int(" 3 ") is 3), but it can't read words or decimals:

ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'three' means "this text doesn't look like a whole number". You'll get the same error for "2.5"; use float() when decimals are allowed. Module 5 shows how to keep asking until the answer is valid.

#f-strings: output that looks the way you want

Put an f before the opening quote and you can drop any variable or calculation into the text inside { }. Add a colon and a format spec after it to control how the value looks:

Line by line: without a spec, 49.0 looks wrong for money. :.2f means "a float with exactly 2 decimal places". In the third line, :<14 pads the item to 14 characters, lined up on the left; :>3 pads the quantity to 3 characters, lined up on the right; and :>8.2f does both jobs at once. Lining values up in fixed widths is how you print tidy columns. :, adds thousands separators.

Spec Meaning
.2f exactly 2 decimal places
>6 right-align in 6 characters
<6 left-align in 6 characters
^7 center in 7 characters
>8.2f both at once: 2 decimals, right-aligned in 8 characters

Here they are applied to the same number. The square brackets are there only to show where the padding spaces go:

f-strings also save you from a classic crash. Gluing text to a number with + doesn't work, because Python won't guess whether you meant math or text:

Write f"Stickers: {stickers}" instead, or use str(stickers).

⚠️ Watch out

Three mistakes to look out for in this module:

  1. Calling a method without storing the result: email.lower() on its own changes nothing. Write email = email.lower().
  2. Doing math on input() without converting it. If a number comes out strangely repeated (33, 555), you forgot int() or float().
  3. Using int() on something that might have a decimal point. int("2.5") crashes; float("2.5") works.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1What does "Chess"[1:3] give?

  • That would be [0:2]. Index 1 is the second character, because counting starts at 0.

  • It takes indexes 1 and 2 (h and e) and stops before index 3.

  • The slice stops before the second number, so index 3 isn't included.

Show answer

B. It takes indexes 1 and 2 (h and e) and stops before index 3.

2name = " Leo ", then name.strip(), then print(len(name)). What prints?

  • That's the length of the stripped copy, but it was never stored back into name.

  • .strip() made a new string and it was thrown away. name still has its 3 spaces, so it's 6 characters.

  • It's true that strings can't be changed, but calling .strip() is fine; it just returns a new string.

Show answer

B. .strip() made a new string and it was thrown away. name still has its 3 spaces, so it's 6 characters.

3A user types 2.5 at int(input("Hours? ")). What happens?

  • int() chops decimals off a float, but it can't read decimal text.

  • int() never produces a decimal.

  • The text "2.5" doesn't look like a whole number to int(). Use float() instead.

Show answer

C. The text "2.5" doesn't look like a whole number to int(). Use float() instead.

4What does f"{3.14159:.2f}" produce?

  • .2f shows the float with exactly two decimal places.

  • That would be .1f.

  • Without a format spec you'd get every digit; the spec is what trims it.

Show answer

A. .2f shows the float with exactly two decimal places.

Key takeaways

  • input() always returns a str. Convert with int() or float() before doing math.
  • Indexes start at 0; a slice [a:b] stops just before b.
  • String methods return new strings. Store the result, or it's lost.
  • in, .isdigit(), and .startswith() answer True or False about text.
  • f-strings with format specs (:.2f, :<10, :>8) control exactly how output looks.

#Further reading

  • String methods (opens in a new tab): the official list of every string method, with a one-paragraph description of each.
  • Formatted string literals (opens in a new tab): the tutorial's section on f-strings, with more format spec examples.
  • Format specification mini-language (opens in a new tab): the full reference for what can go after the colon, for when you need something unusual.

What you'll learn

  • Ask a series of questions with input() and clean every answer before using it.
  • Convert answers to int where you need to do math, and leave them as text where you don't.
  • Build a new piece of text from slices of other strings.
  • Line up a printed slip in columns with f-string widths and .2f.
  • Test a program with messy input on purpose.

People type answers carelessly. They add spaces, forget capital letters, or press Caps Lock halfway through an email address. A good program accepts the mess and tidies it up, so you never see it in the output. You'll build a sign-up program for a school club that does exactly that.

When it's finished, someone who types maya CHEN, robotics, m, and Maya.Chen@School.ORG gets this:

Save a new file as signup_slip.py in your m3 folder.

📝 Note

Each step adds lines to the bottom of the file, and the output shows only the new lines. In Thonny, each run asks all the questions so far, so you'll answer the earlier ones again every time. That's normal while you're building.

#Step 1: Ask for the name and clean it

Three things happen on line 2, from the inside out. input() shows the question and returns whatever was typed, spaces and all. .strip() cuts the spaces off both ends. .title() turns maya CHEN into Maya Chen. The brackets in the print are temporary, there only so you can see that no stray spaces survived. Delete that line once you've checked.

Cleaning at the moment you read the answer means every later line can trust name. If you cleaned it later, you'd have to remember to do it everywhere you used it.

#Step 2: The grade, as a number

Here the answer has to become an int, because the program does math with it. Without int(), 12 - grade would crash with a TypeError, since you can't subtract text from a number. Now compare that with the next step, where none of the answers get converted.

#Step 3: Club, size, email, and newsletter

Each answer gets the cleaning that suits it. Club names look best in title case, sizes are always capitals, and email addresses are conventionally written in lowercase.

The newsletter line is different: it ends with .startswith("y"), which turns the answer into True or False. Lowering it first means Yes, YES, y, and yeah all count as yes. Storing a bool rather than the raw text means the rest of the program never has to worry about how the person spelled it.

#Step 4: The money

DUES and SHIRT_PRICE are written in capitals. Python doesn't treat them any differently, but programmers use capitals for values that are set once and never changed, called constants. In a real project you'd move them to the very top of the file, so next year's treasurer can update the prices without hunting through the code.

Look at the output: 40.0 is correct, but it doesn't look like money. :.2f fixes that by always showing two decimal places.

#Step 5: A member code from slices

The club wants a short code for each member: the first three letters of the club, the grade, and the first three letters of the name, like ROB-9-MAY.

club[:3] slices off the first three characters, Rob, and .upper() capitalizes them. The f-string glues everything together with dashes, and grade goes in without any conversion because f-strings turn numbers into text for you.

This is also why the cleaning in Step 1 mattered. Without .strip(), the slice of " maya CHEN " would be three spaces, and Maya's code would be ROB-9- .

#Step 6: Print the slip

Now line everything up. Each label is padded to 14 characters with :<14, so every value starts in the same column. The money is right-aligned in 8 characters with :>8.2f, so the decimal points line up.

A few details are worth a closer look:

  • "=" * width repeats a character, so you can change the slip's width in one place.
  • {'Name:':<14} puts a plain string inside the braces. It uses single quotes because the f-string itself is in double quotes. Python 3.12 and newer would accept double quotes there too, but older versions (like the one on some Chromebooks) would think the f-string had ended, so mixing the two kinds is the safe habit.
  • {'CLUB SIGN-UP CONFIRMATION':^{width}} centers the title. The width can itself be a {variable} inside the format spec.

#Try to break it

A program isn't finished until you've tried to make it fail. Run your file and try each of these:

Type this Where What happens
SAM lee Name Cleaned to Sam Lee
nope Newsletter False, because it doesn't start with y
XL Size XL, and the space is gone
two Shirts The program crashes

The last one is a real problem:

int() can't turn the word two into a number. In Module 5 you'll make the program ask again instead of crashing. For now, the error message tells you exactly what went wrong and which answer caused it.

#The finished program

The questions now all come first, then the calculations, then the output. Grouping a program into input, processing, output like this makes it much easier to read than mixing the three together.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the program call .strip() on the name before taking name[:3] for the member code?

  • Speed isn't the issue; it's which characters end up in the code.

  • " maya"[:3] is three spaces, so the code would be ROB-9- .

  • Slices work on any string; spaces are just characters like any other.

Show answer

B. " maya"[:3] is three spaces, so the code would be ROB-9- .

2Why is grade converted with int() but size is left as text?

  • You only need a number when you calculate with it, like 12 - grade. A size like M isn't a number at all.

  • int() works on any text that looks like a whole number, wherever it appears.

  • f-strings display integers fine; the slip prints grade directly.

Show answer

A. You only need a number when you calculate with it, like 12 - grade. A size like M isn't a number at all.

3What would {total} show on the slip without :.2f?

  • Python doesn't add trailing zeros unless you ask it to.

  • A float prints with as few decimal places as it needs, which looks odd for money.

  • total is a float (it was built from 15.00 and 12.50), so it keeps a decimal point.

Show answer

B. A float prints with as few decimal places as it needs, which looks odd for money.

Key takeaways

  • Clean each answer the moment you read it (.strip() plus .title(), .upper(), or .lower()), so later code can trust it.
  • Convert with int() only when you need to calculate; keep other answers as text.
  • .lower().startswith("y") turns a messy yes/no answer into a reliable True or False.
  • Fixed widths (:<14, :>8.2f) line output up in columns.
  • Test with messy and wrong input on purpose; the crashes you find are the next things to fix.

#Make it yours

  • Add a question for the person's favorite activity in the club and show it on the slip.
  • Offer a sibling discount: ask how many siblings are already members, and take $5 off the dues for each one.
  • After Module 4, print Yes or No for the newsletter instead of True or False, and reject grades outside 6 to 12.
  • Make the slip 40 characters wide by changing one number. Check that everything still lines up.

  • Fancier output formatting (opens in a new tab): the official tutorial on f-strings, padding, and other ways to lay out printed text.
  • String methods (opens in a new tab): look up .strip(), .title(), and the dozens of others for when you need a different kind of cleaning.

  • Fix ValueError and TypeError crashes caused by mixing text and numbers.

Save each exercise as its own file in your m3 folder. When an exercise reads input, run it at least twice: once with tidy answers and once with messy ones (extra spaces, odd capitals).

Warm-up. In the Shell, type len(" hi ") and then len(" hi ".strip()). Predict both numbers first. Spaces are characters too.

#Exercise 1: Predict the string results

Write down what each line prints, then run it to check:

Need a hint?

Write the word out with its indexes underneath (T is 0, h is 1, and so on). For line 3, think about what .upper() does to the lowercase ns before they're counted.

Show solution

word[0] is T and word[-1] is y, and + joins them. [1:4] takes indexes 1, 2 and 3. .upper() makes THONNY, which has two capital Ns; without it, count("N") would find none, because the original word's ns are lowercase. word * 2 is ThonnyThonny, which has 12 characters.

#Exercise 2: Name badge

Ask for a first name and a last name, then print a badge with the initials underneath. It must look right even when the person types ada and LOVELACE .

Need a hint?

Clean each answer as you read it with .strip().title(). The first letter of a string is at index 0.

Show solution

If you skipped .strip(), first[0] would be a space and the initials would come out as ( .L.). Cleaning first makes every later step simpler.

#Exercise 3: Fix the storage checker

This program estimates how many more photos fit on a phone, at about 300 photos per gigabyte. Run it with the answer 12.5:

Fix it so that typing 12.5 prints Room for about 3,750 more photos. There are two bugs; the second only shows up after you fix the first.

Need a hint?

First: which converter accepts text with a decimal point? Second: you can't join text and a number with +. An f-string with :, can also add the comma, and int() can drop the .0 from a float.

Show solution

int("12.5") raises a ValueError because that text isn't a whole number, so float() is the right converter. Once that's fixed, "Room for about " + photos raises a TypeError, because + can't join a string and a number. The f-string solves that, and int() turns 3750.0 into 3750, so nobody sees a decimal point in a count of photos.

#Exercise 4: Line up the race results

Three runners finished a 400 m race in 61.237, 59.8, and 62.05 seconds. Store each name and time in variables, then print a table where the names line up on the left and the times line up on the right, all with two decimal places:

Need a hint?

Each line is two columns: the name left-aligned in 10 characters (:<10) and the time right-aligned in 10 characters with 2 decimals (:>10.2f). Format the heading the same way so it lines up too.

Show solution

.2f rounds 61.237 to 61.24 and pads 59.8 to 59.80, so every time has the same number of characters and the decimal points sit in one column. The first lines use the two-at-once assignment from Module 2 to keep each runner's name and time together.

#Exercise 5: Username maker

A school makes usernames from the first three letters of your first name, the first letter of your last name, and the last two digits of the year you were born, all in lowercase. Ask for all three and print the username.

Need a hint?

Every part is a slice: [:3], [0], and [-2:]. Should the birth year be converted with int()? Think about whether you'll do math with it or slice it.

Show solution

The year stays a string on purpose. You can slice text, but numbers don't have characters to slice: int("2011")[-2:] crashes with TypeError: 'int' object is not subscriptable. Convert only when you need to calculate.

#Exercise 6: How long will the download take?

Internet speed is measured in megabits per second (Mbps), but file sizes are in megabytes (MB), and one byte is 8 bits. Ask for a file size in MB and a speed in Mbps, and print the time in seconds and in minutes:

Need a hint?

Seconds = size × 8 ÷ speed. Both answers can have decimals, so use float(). To print 25 rather than 25.0, the format spec :g drops a pointless .0. Use :.0f for seconds and :.1f for minutes.

Show solution

Python works left to right through size * 8 / speed: 750 × 8 is 6000 megabits, and 6000 ÷ 25 is 240 seconds. Try a 4200 MB game update on a 100 Mbps connection; it should come out at 336 seconds, or 5.6 minutes.

#Challenge: A banner that fits any message

Ask for a short message and print it in capitals, inside a box of stars that is exactly the right width, with a blank row above and below:

Type Python rocks instead, and the box must stretch to fit. Don't count the characters yourself; make the program do it.

Need a hint?

Each row inside the box is "* ", then something as long as the message, then " *". So the full width is len(message) + 4. "*" * width makes the top row, and " " * len(message) makes the blank space inside.

Show solution

Every row is built from len(message), so the box always fits. The + 4 covers the star and space on each side. Step through it below to watch width get worked out from the message's length.

m4-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Use // and % together to split a number into groups and leftovers.
  • Predict the order Python does arithmetic in, and use brackets to change it.
  • Write comparisons that produce True or False.
  • Choose between paths with if, elif, and else, in the right order.
  • Combine conditions with and, or, and not, and avoid the or trap.
  • Test a decision at, just below, and just above each cutoff.

A phone game promises a bonus life when you reach 1000 points. A player scores exactly 1000:

No bonus life. The rule said reach 1000, but the code checks for more than 1000, and those disagree at exactly one number. Players at 999 and 1001 get the right result; only the player sitting on the line gets cheated. Most decision bugs look like this: one character wrong, at the edge. By the end of this page you'll know how to write the decision and how to catch the bug before a player does.

#Seven ways to do arithmetic

You know +, -, and *. Python has four more, and two of them come as a pair. Here they are with 23 students and vans that hold 7:

Operator Name With 23 and 7 What it's for
/ division 3.2857… An exact answer, always a float
// floor division 3 How many whole groups fit
% remainder (modulo) 2 What's left over after the whole groups
** power 23 ** 2 is 529 Squares, cubes, compound growth

Here's the intuition for the pair: deal 23 students into vans of 7. You fill 23 // 7 = 3 vans and have 23 % 7 = 2 students standing on the curb. Every time you see "how many full ones, and how many left over" (eggs in cartons, minutes in an hour, items per page), reach for // and % together.

% has a second job you'll use constantly: n % 2 is 0 when n is even and 1 when it's odd, and more generally n % k == 0 means n divides exactly by k.

#Which operation happens first

Python follows the same order as math class: ** first, then *, /, //, and %, then + and -. Operations at the same level go left to right. This catches people out when averaging:

The first line divides only quiz2 by 2 and then adds 90, giving 130.0. Brackets force the addition to happen first. If you're ever unsure, add brackets: they never hurt, and they make your meaning obvious to the next reader.

#Comparisons answer True or False

A comparison asks a question about two values and the answer is always a bool:

Operator Asks Example Result
== equal? 5 == 5.0 True
!= not equal? "Owl" != "owl" True
<, > less than, greater than 999 > 1000 False
<=, >= less/greater than or equal 1000 >= 1000 True

Two things to notice. Text comparison is exact, so "Owl" == "owl" is False; that's why Module 3 had you .lower() answers before checking them. And Python lets you chain comparisons the way you'd write them in math: 13 <= age <= 19 is True for teenagers.

The single = stores a value and the double == compares, and mixing them up is a mistake everyone makes once:

Python even suggests the fix in the message.

#if: run some lines only when something is true

An if statement has a condition, a colon, and an indented block underneath. The block runs only when the condition is True. The first line that isn't indented runs either way. The vans need one extra van when there are leftovers:

The indentation is the grammar: it's how Python knows which lines belong to the if. Use 4 spaces. Thonny adds them for you when you press Enter after a colon. Forget them and the program won't start:

#elif and else: pick exactly one path

The UV index tells you how strong the sun is. The World Health Organization's bands are 0 to 2 low, 3 to 5 moderate, 6 to 7 high, 8 to 10 very high, and 11 or more extreme. A chain of if, elif ("else if"), and else picks one message:

Here's the precise rule. Python tests the conditions from the top down. The first one that's True gets its block run, and every branch below it is skipped, even ones that would also be true. If none is true, else runs. Step through it with a UV index of 9 and watch which lines get visited:

Nine is also >= 6 and >= 3, but those lines are never checked. That's why order matters. Put the checks the other way round and the program breaks:

9 >= 3 is true, so the first branch wins and "Very high" can never be reached by anyone. With >= chains, start from the highest cutoff and work down.

#and, or, not: combine conditions

Real rules often have several parts. A school study room is open every day except Sunday, from 8:00 until 21:00:

  • and is True only when both sides are true.
  • or is True when at least one side is true.
  • not flips True to False and back, so not is_member means "isn't a member".

🧪 Try it yourself

Change hour to 21, then to 8, then change day to "Sunday". Predict each result before you run it. Is the room open at 21:00 exactly?

Now the trap. This looks like it checks for the weekend:

It says Tuesday is the weekend. Python reads it as (day == "Saturday") or ("Sunday"). The left side is False, so Python looks at the right side on its own, and any non-empty string counts as true. The fix is to write the full comparison on both sides: day == "Saturday" or day == "Sunday".

#Boundary testing: check the edges

Decision bugs hide at the cutoffs, because that's where > and >= disagree. So don't test random numbers: for each cutoff, test just below it, exactly on it, and just above it. For the bonus life, that's 999, 1000, and 1001, and the 1000 test catches the bug instantly.

For the UV program, the cutoffs are 3, 6, 8, and 11:

Test Expected Why this one
2, 3 Low, Moderate Either side of the first cutoff
5, 6 Moderate, High Either side of the second
7, 8 High, Very high Either side of the third
10, 11 Very high, Extreme Either side of the last
0 Low The smallest real value
-4 ??? Impossible input: what should happen?

The last row matters too. The program says a UV index of -4 is "Low", which is wrong in a different way: the input is impossible. A careful program checks for impossible values first, and the build-along in the next lesson does exactly that.

⚠️ Watch out

Three mistakes to check for in every decision:

  1. = where you meant ==. Python stops with a syntax error, which at least makes it easy to find.
  2. A missing colon at the end of the if line, or a block that isn't indented.
  3. x == "a" or "b". Write the comparison out in full on both sides of or.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A recipe makes 12 cookies per batch. How do you work out the cookies left over when you have dough for 50?

  • That gives 4.1666…, a float, which doesn't tell you how many cookies are left.

  • That gives 4, the number of full batches, not the leftovers.

  • 4 full batches use 48, leaving 2. % gives exactly that remainder.

Show answer

C. 4 full batches use 48, leaving 2. % gives exactly that remainder.

2With temp = 30, what does this print? if temp > 10: → print("Mild"), elif temp > 25: → print("Hot").

  • 30 > 10 is true, so the first branch runs and the elif is never checked.

  • 30 is above 25, but Python stops at the first true condition, and that came earlier.

  • An if/elif chain runs at most one branch.

Show answer

A. 30 > 10 is true, so the first branch runs and the elif is never checked.

3A rule says "free entry for under-5s". Which values best test if age < 5:?

  • These never get close to the cutoff, so they can't tell < from <=.

  • Just below, exactly on, and just above the cutoff: 5 is the value that shows whether the rule is right.

  • 5 matters most, but checking the values beside it confirms the rest of the rule too.

Show answer

B. Just below, exactly on, and just above the cutoff: 5 is the value that shows whether the rule is right.

4fruit = "kiwi". What does if fruit == "apple" or "pear": do?

  • That's what it looks like it means, but Python reads "pear" as a separate condition.

  • A non-empty string is truthy, so the or is always true. Write fruit == "apple" or fruit == "pear".

  • It's valid Python, which is what makes the bug sneaky.

Show answer

B. A non-empty string is truthy, so the or is always true. Write fruit == "apple" or fruit == "pear".

Key takeaways

  • // counts whole groups and % gives the leftover; together they split a number.
  • ** comes first, then *, /, //, %, then + and -; use brackets when in doubt.
  • == compares and = stores. A comparison always produces True or False.
  • In an if/elif/else chain, only the first true branch runs, so with >= order from the highest cutoff down.
  • Write out both comparisons around or: x == "a" or x == "b".
  • Test every cutoff just below, exactly on, and just above, and try impossible input.

#Further reading

  • if statements in the official tutorial (opens in a new tab): a short official example of an if/elif/else chain.
  • Comparisons (opens in a new tab) and Boolean operations (opens in a new tab): the exact rules for ==, <, and, or, and not, including why or can return a string.
  • CS50's notes on conditionals (opens in a new tab): Harvard's write-up of the same ideas, with more worked examples.
