m4-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Turn written pricing rules into constants and calculations.
  • Choose a rate with if/else and a discount with conditions joined by and.
  • Decide between > and >= by reading what a rule really says.
  • Reject impossible input before doing any math.
  • Build a boundary-test table and use it to check every rule.

Riverton, a made-up city, has a bike-share scheme, and it needs a program that prices each ride. Here are its rules, exactly as the city wrote them:

  • Every ride costs a $1.25 unlock fee, plus a per-minute charge: $0.15 for a classic bike, $0.30 for an e-bike.
  • Members pay no unlock fee, and their first 45 minutes on a classic bike are free.
  • Rides longer than 180 minutes pay a $10.00 late fee.
  • A ride must last at least 1 minute, and the bike must be classic or ebike.

Here's the order the finished program makes its decisions in:

And here's what a member who rides a classic bike for 50 minutes will see:

Save a new file as bike_fare.py in your m4 folder. This time every step shows the whole program so far, because the new code often goes in the middle, not at the bottom.

#Step 1: One kind of bike, no discounts

Start with the simplest rider: a non-member on a classic bike.

The prices go in capitalized constants at the top, so a price change means editing one line. In UNLOCK_FEE + minutes * CLASSIC_RATE, Python multiplies first (30 × 0.15 = 4.50) and then adds the 1.25, which is exactly what the rule says. Check it against the rule by hand before moving on; that one habit catches a surprising number of bugs.

#Step 2: Classic or e-bike

Now the rate depends on the bike, so the program has to choose:

The rider typed E-Bike with spaces and a capital and a dash, and it still worked. .strip() removed the spaces, .lower() made it e-bike, and .replace("-", "") removed the dash to give ebike. All the cleaning happens on one line, so the if only ever has to compare against one spelling.

The if/else sets a variable called rate, and the calculation below uses rate without caring which branch set it. That's a pattern worth copying: let the decision pick a value, then do the math once.

#Step 3: Members

Members get two perks, and each one is a separate decision. Add the third question, then replace the fare calculation with the new section:

The free-minutes chain has three cases. A member on a classic bike riding more than 45 minutes pays for the minutes beyond 45. A member on a classic bike riding 45 minutes or less pays for none. Everyone else pays for every minute.

The elif doesn't need to say minutes <= 45. Any member on a classic bike who reaches the elif must have failed the minutes > 45 test above it, so the order of the chain does that work for you. Why not simply subtract 45 for every member on a classic bike? Because a 30-minute ride would then be billed for -15 minutes, and Riverton would owe the rider money.

is_member is already a bool, so if is_member: reads like English. There's no need to write if is_member == True:.

#Step 4: The late fee, and choosing between > and >=

The rule says rides longer than 180 minutes pay the late fee. A ride of exactly 180 minutes is not longer than 180 minutes, so the right comparison is >, not >=. Add the constants and put the late fee check just before the total is printed:

A 181-minute ride gets the fee. Run your own file with 180 and check that it doesn't: the total should be $28.25. Notice the late fee is checked on minutes, the real length of the ride, not billed_minutes. A member's free minutes don't make a long ride any shorter.

#Step 5: Reject impossible rides

Try a ride of 0 minutes or -5 minutes in your current version. It happily prints a fare. And a bike type of scooter is charged as a classic bike, because it falls into the else. Impossible input should get an error message, not a price.

The fix is an if/elif/else around everything after the questions. The two checks come first; all the pricing moves inside the else, so it only runs for valid rides. To move a chunk of code inside, select those lines in Thonny and press Tab (or choose Edit › Indent selected lines). Shift+Tab moves them back out.

Look closely at the bike check: bike != "classic" and bike != "ebike". It means "it's not classic, and it's also not ebike", which is true only for something else. If you wrote or here, every bike would be rejected, because any bike is always "not classic" or "not ebike". When a condition says what something isn't, read it aloud slowly before trusting it.

The if statements inside the else are indented twice as far, and that's fine. Each level of indentation means "this belongs to the line above that ends in a colon".

#Step 6: Test every rule at its edges

The program has four cutoffs: under 1 minute, the 45 free minutes, the 180-minute late limit, and the two valid bike names. Test each one just below, on, and just above. Here's a table with the answers worked out by hand from the rules. Run your file once per row and tick off each one:

Minutes Bike Member Expected total Checks
0 classic no error: at least 1 minute the shortest ride
1 classic no $1.40 just above it
45 classic yes $0.00 exactly the free limit
46 classic yes $0.15 one minute past it
50 ebike yes $15.00 free minutes are classic only
180 classic no $28.25 exactly the late limit: no fee
181 classic no $38.40 one minute over: fee added
200 classic yes $33.25 member discount and late fee
30 E-Bike no $10.25 messy typing still works
20 scooter no error: no such bike unknown bike type

If any row disagrees with your program, work out which rule it's testing and look at that part of the code. Writing the expected answer before running is what makes a test useful; if you write it afterwards, you'll just copy whatever the program said.

#The finished program

Check your understanding

3 questions

1The rule says the fee applies to rides "longer than 180 minutes". Why is the check minutes > LATE_LIMIT and not >=?

  • Both operators work with any numbers, constants included.

  • >= would charge the 180-minute rider too. The 180 and 181 boundary tests are what prove you chose correctly.

  • There's no speed difference worth thinking about; the choice is about meaning.

Show answer

B. >= would charge the 180-minute rider too. The 180 and 181 boundary tests are what prove you chose correctly.

2Why do the two error checks come before the pricing code instead of after it?

  • The pricing sits inside the else, so it only runs when both checks pass.

  • if can go anywhere. The order here is a design choice.

  • The point isn't speed; it's that a 0-minute ride shouldn't be charged anything.

Show answer

A. The pricing sits inside the else, so it only runs when both checks pass.

3What would elif bike != "classic" or bike != "ebike": do?

  • Try classic: it's not ebike, so the or is true and the ride is rejected.

  • Every bike is "not classic" or "not ebike" (usually both), so the condition is always true.

  • It does the opposite: it rejects everything.

Show answer

B. Every bike is "not classic" or "not ebike" (usually both), so the condition is always true.

Key takeaways

  • Put every price and limit in a named constant, and check the first calculation against the rules by hand.
  • Let an if/else choose a value, then do the calculation once with that value.
  • Read the rule's wording to choose > or >=; "longer than" and "at least" mean different things.
  • Check for impossible input first and put the real work in the else.
  • x != "a" and x != "b" rejects anything that isn't one of the two; with or it rejects everything.
  • Write expected answers before testing, at just below, on, and just above every cutoff.

#Make it yours

  • Add a third bike type, cargo, at $0.40 a minute, and add rows to the test table for it.
  • Give members 20% off e-bike minutes. Which cutoffs need new tests?
  • Cap the fare: no single ride (before the late fee) costs more than $20.00. What are the boundary values now?
  • Print Thanks for riding, member! for members and Join for free unlocks! for everyone else.

#Further reading

  • More control flow tools (opens in a new tab): the official tutorial on if, elif, and else, plus a preview of the loops in Module 5.
  • Boolean operations: and, or, not (opens in a new tab): the official rules for how Python combines conditions, and which side it checks first.

m4-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Use // and % to split a number into whole groups and leftovers.
  • Order an if/elif chain so the right branch wins.
  • Combine conditions with and and or, using brackets to make the meaning clear.
  • Compare negative numbers correctly.
  • Find decision bugs by testing just below, on, and just above every cutoff.

Save each exercise as its own file in your m4 folder. For every exercise that makes a decision, write down two or three boundary tests and their expected results before you run anything. The solutions list the tests worth trying.

Warm-up. In the Shell, predict and then check 17 // 5, 17 % 5, 2 ** 5, and 10 / 4. Which one gives a float, and why?

#Exercise 1: Egg cartons

A farm packs eggs into cartons of 12. Ask how many eggs there are, then print how many cartons are full, how many eggs are left over, and how many cartons are needed in total (a part-full carton still counts).

Need a hint?

// gives the full cartons and % gives the leftover. You need one extra carton only when the leftover is more than 0. Test with 24 (no leftover) and 5 (no full cartons).

Show solution

With 24 eggs, left is 0, so no extra carton is added and the answer is 2. With 5 eggs, full is 0 and the if adds 1. This "round up when there's a remainder" pattern comes up all the time: buses for a trip, pages for a list, boxes for a delivery.

#Exercise 2: FizzBuzz for one number

FizzBuzz is a classic programming puzzle. Ask for a whole number. Print Fizz if it divides exactly by 3, Buzz if it divides exactly by 5, FizzBuzz if it divides by both, and otherwise the number itself.

Need a hint?

n % 3 == 0 means "divides exactly by 3". Test with 30. If your program prints Fizz, think about which check has to come first.

Show solution

Numbers that divide by both 3 and 5 divide by 15, and they also pass the % 3 test, so the both-at-once check must come first or it would never be reached. Good tests: 9 (Fizz), 10 (Buzz), 30 (FizzBuzz), and 7 (just the number).

#Exercise 3: Can they swim alone?

A public pool's rule: swimmers aged 12 or over can swim on their own. Swimmers aged 8 to 11 can swim on their own if they've passed the swim test. Everyone else needs an adult in the water. Ask for the age and whether they passed the test.

Need a hint?

There are two ways to be allowed: "12 or over", or "8 or over and passed". Turn the yes/no answer into a bool with .strip().lower().startswith("y"), as in Module 3.

Show solution

Python works out and before or, so the brackets aren't strictly needed, but they make the two routes obvious to anyone reading. The boundaries are ages 7, 8, 11 and 12, each with and without the test: 7 with a pass still needs an adult, 8 with a pass doesn't, 11 without a pass does, and 12 never does.

#Exercise 4: Wi-Fi bars

Wi-Fi strength is measured in dBm, and the numbers are negative: -40 is a strong signal and -85 is a weak one. As a rough guide, -50 or higher is 4 bars, -60 or higher is 3, -70 or higher is 2, -80 or higher is 1, and anything lower has no usable signal. A positive number is impossible. Ask for the reading and print the bars.

Need a hint?

-67 is greater than -70, because it's closer to zero. So the comparisons work exactly like the UV index: start with the highest cutoff (-50) and go down. Check for impossible values first.

Show solution

Test each cutoff and the number just past it: -50 and -51, -60 and -61, -70 and -71, -80 and -81. If -51 gives 4 bars, you've used > where you meant >=, or put the checks in the wrong order. Negative numbers feel backwards at first, so it helps to picture a number line: further right means bigger.

#Exercise 5: Shipping costs

An online shop charges $4.99 for standard shipping, but standard shipping is free on orders of $35.00 or more. Express shipping always costs $12.99, whatever the order. Ask for the subtotal and whether the customer wants express, then print the shipping cost and the total.

Need a hint?

Which question decides things first: the order size or express? If someone picks express, the free-shipping rule doesn't matter. Put the prices in constants and test 34.99 and 35.00.

Show solution

Express is checked first because it overrides everything else. Then "$35.00 or more" becomes >=, so an order of exactly $35.00 ships free. Test 34.99 (pays $4.99), 35.00 (free), and an express order of any size (always $12.99).

#Exercise 6: The discount that never gets bigger

A shop gives 10% off orders of $50 or more and 20% off orders of $100 or more. This program has two bugs. Before changing anything, fill in a test table for 49.99, 50, 99.99, 100 and 120, writing what should happen. Then run each one and mark the rows that are wrong.

(:.0% shows a number as a percentage with no decimal places, so 0.1 prints as 10%.)

Need a hint?

Three of your five tests should fail, for two different reasons. An order of $120 should get 20%: why can the elif never run? An order of exactly $50 should get 10%: which word in the rule ("or more") isn't in the code?

Show solution
Order Should get Buggy program gave
49.99 0% 0%
50 10% 0% (wrong)
99.99 10% 10%
100 20% 10% (wrong)
120 20% 10% (wrong)

Bug one is the order: any total over 100 is also over 50, so the 10% branch won every time and 20% was unreachable. Bug two is > instead of >=: "or more" includes the cutoff itself. The 120 test catches the first bug; only the exact-cutoff tests, 50 and 100, catch the second. That's why boundary tests use the cutoff itself, not just numbers near it.

#Challenge: 24-hour to 12-hour clock

Ask for an hour (0 to 23) and a minute (0 to 59) in 24-hour time and print it in 12-hour time with AM or PM. Minutes always have two digits. Reject times that don't exist.

Your program must get these right: 0:05 → 12:05 AM, 9:30 → 9:30 AM, 12:00 → 12:00 PM, 13:45 → 1:45 PM, 23:59 → 11:59 PM, and 24:00 → not a real time.

Need a hint?

hour % 12 turns 13 into 1 and 23 into 11, but it turns both 0 and 12 into 0, and the clock shows 12 for both. The format spec :02d pads a number to two digits with a leading zero, so 5 prints as 05.

Show solution

The validity check uses or because any one bad part makes the time impossible. AM or PM depends only on whether the hour is before noon. % 12 handles every hour except the two that land on 0, midnight and noon, which the final if fixes. The trickiest boundaries are 0, 11, 12 and 13; test all four.

m5-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Write a while loop that keeps asking until the user types a valid answer.
  • Use for with range() and with a list to repeat work a known number of times.
  • Keep a running total, a count, and a best-so-far value inside a loop.
  • Leave a loop early with break, skip a pass with continue, and watch a loop run in Thonny's debugger.

Here is one quiz question, and it has a flaw you won't see until a real person uses it.

The player typed 7, which isn't one of the choices, and the program graded it as a wrong answer anyway. A better program would say "please pick 1, 2, or 3" and ask again. But how many times? Once? Five times? You can't know in advance, so copying and pasting the input() line can never be enough. You need a way to say "repeat this until the answer makes sense." That is what a loop does.

#while: repeat as long as something is true

Think of brushing your teeth: you keep going while they still feel fuzzy. You don't decide on a number of strokes ahead of time; you check, brush, and check again.

Python's while loop works the same way. It checks a condition. If the condition is True, it runs the indented lines underneath (the body), then jumps back up and checks again. The moment the condition is False, Python skips the body and carries on with the rest of the program. Each trip through the body is one iteration.

Before you run this, guess how many "still gaming" lines it prints.

Three lines, not four. After the third pass battery is 10, so battery > 20 is False and the loop ends. The line battery = battery - 30 is what makes the loop finish: every pass moves the battery closer to the stopping point. Python also lets you write that line as battery -= 30, which means exactly the same thing.

#Keep asking until the answer is valid

Now back to the quiz. The fix uses a pattern you'll write over and over in this course, called a validation loop:

  1. Ask once, before the loop.
  2. Loop while the answer is bad: explain the rule, then ask again.
  3. After the loop, you know the answer is good.

choice not in ["1", "2", "3"] is True when the answer matches none of the three allowed strings. The player typed 7, then two, and the loop caught both. Only 2 got through to the if.

Step through it and keep your eye on choice. Notice that the while line is checked three times, but the last line runs only once.

The same shape works for numbers. A string's .isdigit() method gives True only if the string is non-empty and every character is a digit like 0 to 9, which makes it a handy check before you call int():

-3 was turned away because - is not a digit. For an age, that's what you want. (In Module 7 you'll meet try and except, which can also handle negative numbers and decimals.)

#for: repeat once for each item

A while loop runs until something changes. A for loop runs once for each item in a collection, so you know up front how many passes it will make.

The simplest collection is a range of numbers. range(5) gives 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. Give it two numbers and it starts at the first and stops before the second. A third number sets the step size.

The loop variable minute takes each value in turn: 0, 15, 30, 45. It never reaches 60, because range stops before the stop value. Only the indented line repeats; the last line runs once, after the loop.

A for loop can also walk through a list, a sequence of values written inside square brackets and separated by commas. You'll do much more with lists in Module 7. For now, here is the most useful thing a list can do:

Each pass, song holds the next item. len(songs) counts the items. Notice that you never wrote "4" anywhere in the loop; add a fifth song to the list and the loop plays it too.

💡 Tip

Choose loop variable names that describe one item: for song in songs, for minute in range(...). Code like for x in y works, but you'll have to work out what x means every time you read it.

#Running totals, counts, and best-so-far

Loops get useful when each pass adds to something. This is the accumulator pattern: create a variable before the loop, update it inside the loop, and use it after the loop.

Three accumulators share one loop. total adds every game. big_games adds 1 only when a condition is true, so it counts. best changes only when a game beats the record so far. Step through a shorter version and watch both variables change:

On the third pass, game is 7. It gets added to total, but 7 > 18 is False, so best stays at 18.

#break and continue: leave early or skip ahead

Sometimes you don't know how many items are coming, like a coach typing in scores until they're finished. Two keywords help:

  • break ends the loop immediately. Python jumps to the first line after the loop.
  • continue skips the rest of this pass and goes straight back to the top for the next one.

while True would run forever on its own, so the break is the only way out. When the coach pressed Enter on an empty line, continue jumped back to input() without adding anything, which is why the count is 3 and not 4. The :.1f inside the f-string rounds the average to one decimal place.

#Watch a loop run in Thonny

Reading a loop is one thing; seeing it is another. Thonny's debugger lets you run a program one step at a time:

  1. Open View › Variables so the Variables panel is showing.
  2. Start the debugger with Run › Debug current script (nicer), the Debug button on the toolbar, or Ctrl+F5. (On a Mac you may need to hold fn for the F keys.)
  3. Press F6 (Step over) to run one statement at a time. Watch the highlighted line jump back to the while or for after each pass, and watch the values change in the Variables panel.
  4. Press F8 (Resume) to run the rest normally, or the red Stop button to quit.

Try it with basketball.py. Seeing best sit still while total keeps climbing makes the accumulator pattern click.

#Mistakes that trip up everyone

⚠️ Watch out

Forgetting to ask again inside a validation loop. If the input() line only appears before the loop, a bad answer never changes, and the program prints "Please type 1, 2, or 3." forever. Any loop whose condition never becomes False is an infinite loop. In Thonny, click the red Stop button (or press Ctrl+F2) to end it, then make sure the body changes something the condition checks.

⚠️ Watch out

Off by one with range. range(1, 10) gives 1 to 9, not 1 to 10. If you want the last number included, make the stop value one bigger: range(1, 11).

A loop that sometimes runs zero times can also crash code that comes after it. Here the coach types done straight away:

count is still 0, and dividing by zero is not allowed. The fix is a check after the loop: if count > 0: print the average, else: print "No scores entered."

Check your understanding

4 questions

1What does this print? n = 1, then while n < 20: with the body n = n * 3, then print(n) after the loop.

  • 9 is still less than 20, so the loop runs one more time.

  • n goes 1, 3, 9, 27. When n is 27, n < 20 is False, and the loop stops with 27.

  • The condition uses 20 as a limit, but n only ever holds powers of 3.

  • n grows every pass, so the condition eventually becomes False.

Show answer

B. n goes 1, 3, 9, 27. When n is 27, n < 20 is False, and the loop stops with 27.

2Which numbers does for i in range(2, 10, 3): print(i) print?

  • range stops before 10, so 11 is never produced.

  • Start at 2 and add 3 each time: 2, 5, 8. The next value, 11, is past the stop.

  • The first number is where it starts, so 2 comes first.

Show answer

B. Start at 2 and add 3 each time: 2, 5, 8. The next value, 11, is past the stop.

3A validation loop prints "Please type yes or no." over and over without waiting for the user. What is the most likely bug?

  • The answer never changes, so the condition stays True forever.

  • not in is fine; it's the standard way to check for an answer outside the allowed list.

  • You don't know how many tries a person will need, so while is the right loop.

Show answer

A. The answer never changes, so the condition stays True forever.

4In scores.py, what happens if the continue on the blank-line check is changed to break?

  • break doesn't skip; it ends the whole loop.

  • break happens before int(entry), so nothing crashes there.

  • break leaves the loop entirely, so any scores after the blank are never asked for.

Show answer

C. break leaves the loop entirely, so any scores after the blank are never asked for.

Key takeaways

  • A while loop repeats as long as its condition is True; something in the body must eventually make it False.
  • A validation loop asks once before the loop, then asks again inside the loop until the answer passes.
  • A for loop runs once per item in a range or a list; range(start, stop, step) stops before stop.
  • Accumulators start before the loop, change inside it, and are used after it.
  • break leaves a loop now; continue skips to the next pass.

#Further reading

  • Python tutorial: More Control Flow Tools (opens in a new tab): the official explanation of while, for, range(), break, and continue, with short examples.
  • Python docs: str.isdigit() (opens in a new tab): exactly which characters count as digits.
  • Thonny's home page (opens in a new tab): short animations of stepping through code and watching variables.

What you'll learn

  • Combine a for loop (one pass per question) with a while loop (one pass per bad answer).
  • Use random.randint() to make new questions, and random.seed() to make them repeatable while you test.
  • Keep score with accumulators and turn the score into a percentage.
  • Use break to quit early and continue to skip a question.

You're going to build a quick-fire multiplication quiz. It asks five questions, refuses answers like seventy, lets the player skip or quit, and grades them at the end. Here's a session with the finished program, where the player gets one right, skips one, mistypes one, gets one wrong, and then quits:

The program has two loops, one inside the other. The outer for loop runs once per question. The inner while loop runs once per bad answer, which is usually zero times.

Open Thonny, make a new file, and save it as sprint.py in your m5 folder. Type each step in yourself rather than pasting; you'll catch more of your own typos that way.

#Step 1: Ask one question

Start with a single question and fixed numbers, so there's nothing random to confuse you yet.

input() always gives back a string, so int(answer) converts it before comparing. That works for 56. Now try what a real player might type:

int() can't turn the word fifty-six into a number, so the program crashes. The last line of the error names the problem: a ValueError, with the exact text that caused it. A quiz that crashes on a typo isn't fun, so that's the next thing to fix.

#Step 2: Refuse answers that aren't numbers

Add a validation loop between the input() and the if. It keeps asking while the answer isn't made of digits:

By the time Python reaches the if, answer is guaranteed to be all digits, so int(answer) can't crash. The two spaces at the start of the hint message are only there to indent it, so it stands out from the questions.

#Step 3: Five random questions

Now wrap the question in a for loop and let Python pick the numbers. random.randint(2, 12) returns a random whole number from 2 to 12, and unlike range, it includes both ends.

Three things changed:

  • import random at the top loads Python's random module so you can use its functions.
  • Everything about one question moved inside the for loop and got indented one level. The while loop is now indented twice, because it lives inside the for.
  • range(1, 6) gives 1 to 5, so the questions are numbered the way people count.

random.seed(3) deserves a word. Random numbers make testing hard: you can't check an answer if the question changes every run. Seeding the generator with a fixed number makes it produce the same "random" sequence each time, so you'll see 5 x 11 first every run. When the quiz works, delete that line and every game will be different.

🧪 Try it yourself

Change randint(2, 12) to randint(2, 20) and run it again. Then change range(1, 6) to range(1, 11). You just made a harder, longer quiz by editing two numbers.

#Step 4: Keep score

A quiz needs a score. That's an accumulator: create it before the loop, add to it inside the loop, and report it after the loop. While you're at it, replace the magic number 5 with a named constant, ROUNDS, so the question count lives in one place.

score starts at 0 and only grows inside the if branch for correct answers. Names in capital letters, like ROUNDS, are a Python habit meaning "this value is set once and never changed."

Step through a two-question version below. Watch score go up only on the correct answer, and see how the while loop runs once for the typo and zero times otherwise.

#Step 5: Let the player skip or quit

Real players want an exit. The quiz will accept two letters as well as numbers: s skips the current question and q ends the quiz. This is exactly what continue and break are for.

The validation loop needs a new condition: keep asking while the answer is neither a number nor one of the two letters.

.strip() removes stray spaces, and .lower() turns Q into q, so the player doesn't get scolded for pressing Shift. Then:

  • break jumps out of the for loop completely, straight to the score report.
  • continue jumps back to the top of the for loop, so the next question is asked and the grading code below is skipped.
  • A new accumulator, asked, counts questions the player actually tried (answered or skipped). If someone quits after two questions, grading them out of 5 wouldn't be fair.

The order matters here. asked = asked + 1 sits after the quit check (quitting doesn't count as a try) but before the skip check (skipping does).

#Step 6: The finished program

Here's everything together, with a percentage and a message at the end. Run it with the same inputs as the session at the top of this page.

The \n at the end of the second print adds a blank line, and print() with nothing inside prints one too. The if asked == 0 check guards against dividing by zero when someone types q on the very first question:

Test your own copy the way a mischievous friend would: type nothing and press Enter, type -5, type Q with spaces, type 3.5. Every one of those should get a polite hint instead of a crash.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1What would happen if score = 0 were moved to the first line inside the for loop?

  • Nothing adds twice; the line only sets score back to 0.

  • Each new question resets score to 0, so only the last question can count.

  • Setting a variable inside a loop is allowed. The bug is in the logic, not the syntax.

Show answer

B. Each new question resets score to 0, so only the last question can count.

2Why does q use break while s uses continue?

  • break leaves the for loop entirely, while continue goes back to its top for the next question.

  • Both keywords work in for and while loops.

  • Speed isn't the difference; where the program goes next is.

Show answer

A. break leaves the for loop entirely, while continue goes back to its top for the next question.

3A player answers 2 questions and then types q. Why is the score shown "out of 2" rather than "out of 5"?

  • ROUNDS is never changed; it stays 5.

  • asked goes up once per answered or skipped question, and quitting happens before that line.

  • break doesn't reset anything; it just stops the loop.

Show answer

B. asked goes up once per answered or skipped question, and quitting happens before that line.

Key takeaways

  • A for loop handles "once per question"; a while loop inside it handles "until the answer is valid."
  • random.randint(a, b) includes both a and b; random.seed() makes the sequence repeatable for testing.
  • Constants like ROUNDS keep a number in one place, so changing the quiz length is a one-line edit.
  • break ends the whole loop and continue ends one pass; place your accumulator updates with that in mind.
  • Guard any division that comes after a loop, in case the loop ran zero times.

#Make it yours

  • Mix the operations. Pick an operator with op = random.choice(["+", "-", "x"]) and compute the right answer with if/elif. (Watch out: subtraction can give negative answers, which .isdigit() rejects. Keep a bigger than b.)
  • Three lives. Replace the fixed number of rounds with a while lives > 0: loop that ends after three wrong answers.
  • Speed bonus. import time, record time.time() before and after each answer, and award a bonus point for answers under 3 seconds.
  • Difficulty levels. Ask for easy, medium, or hard at the start (with a validation loop, of course) and set the randint range from the answer.

#Further reading

  • Python docs: the random module (opens in a new tab): randint, choice, seed, and the rest, with examples near the bottom of the page.
  • Python tutorial: break and continue (opens in a new tab): the official short explanation, including the else clause that loops can have.
  • Python docs: string methods (opens in a new tab): look up strip, lower, and isdigit, three methods you'll use in almost every input loop.

m5-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Pick the right loop for a job: for when you know how many passes, while when you don't.
  • Validate input with a while loop that checks both the type and the range of an answer.
  • Use counters, totals, best-so-far values, and flags inside loops.
  • Use break and continue to control a loop that reads until the user is finished.

Each exercise has a sample of what your program should print. Write your own version in Thonny first, run it, and compare. Open a hint only if you're stuck for more than a few minutes, and the solution only after you've tried. If your output doesn't match, step through with Ctrl+F5 and F6 and watch the Variables panel.

#Warm-up: predict three ranges

Before you run anything, write down what each loop prints. print(i, end=" ") puts a space after each number instead of starting a new line.

Show solution

Every range stops before its stop value: 4 is missing from the first line, 8 from the second, and 0 from the third. The empty print() calls end each line.

#Exercise 1: Count down by twos

Print the even numbers from 10 down to 0, then Lift-off!. Use one for loop and no if.

Need a hint?

range takes a third number, the step, and a negative step counts down. The stop value is never included, so to reach 0 you need to stop one past it.

Show solution

The stop is -1, so 0 is the last number produced. With a stop of 0 the loop would end at 2.

#Exercise 2: A star rating from 1 to 5

Ask the user to rate a movie from 1 to 5. Keep asking until they type a whole number in that range, then print that many stars.

Need a hint?

The loop should keep going if the text is not all digits, or if the number is below 1, or above 5. Put the .isdigit() check first: Python stops reading an or as soon as one part is True, so int() never sees six. And "*" * 4 gives "****".

Show solution

Swap the order to int(text) < 1 or not text.isdigit() and type six: the program crashes with a ValueError, because int() runs before the digit check gets a chance.

#Exercise 3: How long is the playlist?

Song lengths are stored in seconds. Print the total length in minutes and seconds, plus the length of the longest track.

Need a hint?

Use two accumulators in one loop: a running total that starts at 0, and a longest-so-far that changes only when a song beats it. After the loop, // gives whole minutes and % gives the seconds left over.

Show solution

1122 seconds is 18 full minutes (1080 seconds) with 42 left over. Python also has built-in sum() and max() functions that would do this in one line each, but writing the loop yourself shows you what they do inside.

#Exercise 4: The first heat warning

A greenhouse sensor logs one temperature per hour. Find the first hour when it goes above 35°C, print a warning, and stop checking. If it never goes above 35, print No heat warnings today. Hours are numbered from 1.

Need a hint?

Keep an hour counter that goes up by 1 every pass. You also need a flag: a variable like found = False before the loop that you set to True when you find a hot reading. After the loop, the flag tells you whether to print the "no warnings" message.

Show solution

break stops the loop at hour 4, so 38 is never checked and you get exactly one warning. Change the list to [24, 27, 31] and the flag stays False, so the second message appears instead.

#Exercise 5: A word collector

You're collecting words for a word game. Keep asking for words until the user presses Enter on an empty line. Reject words shorter than 3 letters with a message. At the end, print how many words were kept and the longest one.

Need a hint?

Use while True:. An empty answer means break. A short word means print the message and continue, so the counting code below doesn't run. len(word) gives the number of letters. What should the program print if no words were kept at all?

Show solution

longest starts as the empty string, which has length 0, so the first kept word always replaces it.

#Exercise 6: The doubling penny

Someone offers you a deal: 1 cent today, 2 cents tomorrow, 4 the day after, doubling every day. On which day does that day's payment first go over $1,000,000? How much have you collected in total by then?

Need a hint?

You don't know how many days it takes, so use while. Work in cents to avoid decimal surprises: keep day, today (cents paid that day), and total. Loop while today is at most 100,000,000 cents. To print dollars with commas, divide by 100 and use :,.2f in the f-string.

Show solution

Python lets you write 100_000_000 with underscores so big numbers are easier to read. Notice the total is always one cent less than twice the day's payment; doubling grows that fast.

#Challenge: Hailstone numbers

Pick any positive whole number and follow two rules: if it's even, halve it; if it's odd, multiply by 3 and add 1. Repeat until you reach 1. The numbers bounce up and down like hailstones in a storm cloud. Mathematicians believe every starting number eventually reaches 1, but nobody has managed to prove it (it's called the Collatz conjecture).

Write a program that asks for a starting number (validated: whole and greater than 0), prints the path on one line, and reports how many steps it took.

Here's the loop's shape. The validation loop comes first, before any of this.

Step through the path from 6 and watch n climb to 16 before it falls:

Need a hint?

n % 2 == 0 is True for even numbers. Use // (not /) to halve, so n stays a whole number instead of turning into 3.0. Print the starting number with end=" " before the loop, then print each new n the same way inside it.

Show solution

Starting from 27, the path takes 111 steps and climbs as high as 9232 before falling back to 1. Try 97 and 871 next. The highest accumulator is an extra; it uses the same best-so-far pattern as Exercise 3.

m6-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Define a function with def and call it as many times as you need.
  • Pass values in with parameters, including default values and keyword arguments.
  • Send a result back with return, and explain why print inside a function is not the same thing.
  • Predict which variables a function can see, and document a function with a docstring.

This workout summary has the same three lines of math pasted three times. Look closely at the output:

5:7 should be 5:07. The first two copies use :02d, which pads a number to two digits with a leading zero, but whoever pasted the third copy dropped it. This is the real cost of copy and paste: every copy is a separate place for a bug to hide, and fixing one copy doesn't fix the others. A function gives the logic one home, so you write it once, test it once, and fix it once.

#One copy instead of three: def

Here's the same program with the time math moved into a function:

Read the first line piece by piece:

  • def tells Python you're defining a function.
  • format_time is its name. Use the same naming rules as variables, and pick a verb or a description of what it gives back.
  • (total_seconds) is the parameter: a variable that will hold whatever value the caller passes in.
  • The colon and the indented block form the body, the code that runs each time the function is called.

Defining a function doesn't run its body. Python just remembers it. The body runs when you call the function by writing its name with parentheses, like format_time(307). The value inside the parentheses at the call is the argument, and it becomes the parameter's value for that call.

Step through this and watch the stack on the right. Each call adds a new box (a frame) with its own variables. When the call returns, the box disappears and its answer lands in the variable on the left.

Notice that the trace jumps from line 1 straight to line 6 at the start. Python reads the def and moves on; it only enters the body at the call.

#Parameters carry values in

A function can take several parameters, separated by commas. Arguments match parameters by position: first to first, second to second. You can also give a parameter a default value, used when the caller leaves it out.

Line by line:

  • Three arguments fill all three parameters.
  • Rook gets the default level=1 because no third argument was passed.
  • Keyword arguments (name="Wren") match by name, so their order doesn't matter.
  • The last call swaps the first two arguments. Python can't tell that's a mistake; it just matches by position and produces nonsense.

Leave out a parameter that has no default and Python refuses to run the call:

The message names the function and the exact parameter that's missing, which makes this one of the friendlier errors to fix.

#return sends a value back (and print doesn't)

print shows text to the person at the screen. return hands a value back to the code that made the call, so that code can store it, add it up, compare it, or pass it to another function. They look similar when you test in the Shell, which is why they get confused so often.

The return version works. The print version shows 10.8 and 5.4, then crashes. A function with no return gives back a special value called None, so Python ends up trying to compute None + None. Read the last line of the error with that in mind: NoneType is the type of None.

return also ends the function on the spot. That lets you write a chain of checks without elif, because the first one that matches stops everything else:

For 70 km/h the first if returns "gale" and the other checks never run.

#Variables inside a function stay inside

Variables created inside a function, including its parameters, are local. They're created when the call starts and thrown away when it ends. Code outside the function can't see them:

The function worked and printed 1:35, but minutes vanished when the call ended. This is a feature: you can use simple names like minutes inside many functions without them overwriting each other.

The flip side surprises nearly everyone. Predict what this prints before you step through it:

There are two separate variables called coins: one in the Global frame and one in the collect() frame. The function changes its own copy to 15, and the outside one stays at 10. The fix is the rule that makes functions easy to reason about: values go in through parameters and come out through return.

#Docstrings say what a function is for

A docstring is a string in triple quotes on the first line of the body. Python stores it with the function, and help() prints it:

A good docstring says what goes in, what comes out, and gives one example. Write it before the body and you'll often find you understand the function better before you've typed a line of it.

#Step into a function in Thonny

In the debugger, F6 (Step over) runs a whole function call in one go. F7 (Step into) goes inside it. Thonny opens the call in its own small window, with a separate table of local variables and its own highlighted line, so you can see exactly what this call is working with. Run workout_v2.py with Ctrl+F5, then press F7 when you reach a call to format_time.

#Mistakes worth recognizing on sight

⚠️ Watch out

Calling a function before Python has read its def. Python runs a file from top to bottom, so a call on line 1 to a function defined on line 5 fails with NameError: name '...' is not defined. Put your function definitions at the top of the file and the code that uses them below.

⚠️ Watch out

Forgetting the parentheses. print(format_time) doesn't call the function; it prints something like <function format_time at 0x10a3f2e80>, which is Python describing the function itself. If you see that, add the parentheses and the argument.

⚠️ Watch out

Printing when you meant to return. If a calculation shows the right number but then the next line crashes with something about NoneType, look for a print where a return should be.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1What does this print? def double(n): with the body n * 2, then print(double(4)).

  • The body calculates 8, but nothing sends it back.

  • There's no return, so the function gives back None, and that's what gets printed.

  • Calculating a value and not using it is allowed; it just gets thrown away.

Show answer

B. There's no return, so the function gives back None, and that's what gets printed.

2This program has def greet(): with the body print("A"), then print("B"), then greet(). What appears, in order?

  • The def only defines greet; its body doesn't run until the call on the last line.

  • Python skips over the body when it reads the def, prints B, and then prints A when greet() is called.

  • greet() on the last line does call the function, so A is printed too.

Show answer

B. Python skips over the body when it reads the def, prints B, and then prints A when greet() is called.

3x = 5, then def bump(x): with the body x = x + 1 and return x, then bump(x) and print(x). What prints?

  • bump changes its own local x and returns 6, but the result isn't stored, so the global x is still 5.

  • You'd need x = bump(x) to keep the 6.

  • A parameter can share a name with a global variable; they're separate variables.

Show answer

A. bump changes its own local x and returns 6, but the result isn't stored, so the global x is still 5.

4Which call to def describe_hero(name, power, level=1) gives "Ivy (level 1) uses vines!"?

  • Arguments match by position, so this makes "vines" the name.

  • Keyword arguments match by name, so order doesn't matter, and level uses its default.

  • power has no default, so this raises a TypeError.

Show answer

B. Keyword arguments match by name, so order doesn't matter, and level uses its default.

Key takeaways

  • def name(parameters): defines a function; the body only runs when you call name(arguments).
  • Arguments match parameters by position unless you use keyword arguments; defaults fill in anything left out.
  • return hands a value back and ends the call. With no return, a function gives back None.
  • Variables inside a function are local to that call. Pass values in with parameters and get results out with return.
  • A docstring on the first line of the body explains the function, and help() shows it.

#Further reading

  • Python tutorial: Defining Functions (opens in a new tab): the official introduction, followed by more on default values and keyword arguments.
  • PEP 257: Docstring Conventions (opens in a new tab): how Python programmers agree to write docstrings. The one-line docstring section is all you need for now.
  • Python FAQ: arguments vs parameters (opens in a new tab): a two-paragraph answer to a question that confuses beginners and experts alike.

What you'll learn

  • Split a program into small functions that each do one job and return one result.
  • Test each function on its own before connecting them.
  • Write one validation function and reuse it with different limits.
  • Read a short traceback that passes through a function, and fix the bug it points to.

Runners talk about pace: how long each kilometre takes. Finish a 5K in 27 minutes and 5 seconds and your pace is 5:25 per km. Today you'll build a calculator that works that out and then predicts your time for other races at the same pace. Here's the finished program in action, including two typos it catches:

The program is six small functions plus a short main section that calls them. Each arrow below is a value being passed in or returned.

Function Takes Gives back
ask_whole_number(prompt, low, high) a question and the allowed range a valid int
race_name(choice) 1, 2, or 3 "5K", "10K", or "Half marathon"
race_km(choice) 1, 2, or 3 5, 10, or 21.0975
to_seconds(minutes, seconds) two whole numbers total seconds
pace_per_km(total_seconds, km) a time and a distance seconds per km
format_time(total_seconds) a number of seconds text like "5:25"

Planning the functions like this before writing code is worth the two minutes it takes. Each row is a promise: give it this, and it gives back that.

#Step 1: Time conversion, tested first

Start a new Thonny file, pace.py, in your m6 folder, with the two functions that deal with time. Test them immediately with calls whose answers you already know.

Printing the expected answer next to the real one is a quick, honest test. If a line doesn't match, you know exactly which function to look at, before it's buried inside a bigger program.

#Step 2: Pace, and a bug

Pace is total time divided by distance. Add the function and test it with the 5K example:

Read the error from the bottom up. The last line says a ValueError happened because the format code d doesn't work for a float. The line above it points inside format_time, at the f-string. And the line above that shows where format_time was called from.

Now look at the first line of output: pace is 325.0. Dividing with / always gives a float, even when the answer is a whole number. format_time was tested with whole numbers only, and :02d means "a whole number, padded to 2 digits," so a float breaks it.

The fix belongs inside format_time, so every caller benefits: round the input to the nearest whole second first. While you're there, add hours, because a half marathon takes well over 60 minutes.

round() with one argument gives back an int, so the rest of the function is back to whole-number math. total_seconds % 3600 // 60 takes the seconds left after removing whole hours, then counts the whole minutes in them.

#Step 3: One validation function for every question

The program asks three questions with different limits: race 1 to 3, minutes 0 to 300, seconds 0 to 59. Instead of writing three validation loops, write one function and pass the limits in as parameters.

This is the validation loop from Module 5, wrapped in a function. The return int(text) at the end matters: the function's job is to hand back a clean number, not just to display one.

Step through it and watch the ask_whole_number() frame. Its low and high change between the two calls, and text disappears each time a call returns.

#Step 4: The race menu and the predictions

Two tiny functions turn a menu number into a name and a distance. Each uses early returns, so there's no need for elif.

A half marathon is 21.0975 km, half of the 42.195 km marathon. Because ask_whole_number guarantees the choice is 1, 2, or 3, these functions don't need to check for anything else.

The test loop at the bottom is the prediction feature in rough form: one pass per race, calling the same two functions each time. The half marathon comes out as 6856.6875 seconds, which is exactly why format_time rounds before it does anything else. In the finished program, format_time(finish) replaces the raw number.

#Step 5: The finished calculator

Put the functions at the top and the main program at the bottom. The main section reads almost like a description of what the program does, because each function's name says what it does.

Try a half marathon too. Run it in Thonny and type 3, 115, and 30; you should see a pace of 5:28 per km. The if total == 0 check exists because 0 minutes and 0 seconds are both valid answers on their own, but together they'd make a meaningless race.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does ask_whole_number take low and high as parameters instead of always checking 0 to 59?

  • Parameters turn fixed values into choices the caller makes, so one function covers all three questions.

  • A function can have any number of parameters, including none.

  • Speed isn't the point; avoiding three copies of the same loop is.

Show answer

A. Parameters turn fixed values into choices the caller makes, so one function covers all three questions.

2The float bug was fixed by adding round() inside format_time. Why there, and not before each call?

  • round() works anywhere.

  • If each caller had to remember to round first, the next one you write could forget and bring the bug back.

  • It can, and does; that's what exposed the bug.

Show answer

B. If each caller had to remember to round first, the next one you write could forget and bring the bug back.

3Suppose ask_whole_number ended with print(int(text)) instead of return int(text). What happens to minutes = ask_whole_number("Finish time, minutes: ", 0, 300)?

  • print only shows the value; it doesn't send it back.

  • Without return, the function gives back None, and the math fails a few lines later.

  • The function runs fine; the problem only appears when its result is used.

Show answer

B. Without return, the function gives back None, and the math fails a few lines later.

Key takeaways

  • Plan the functions first: for each one, decide what it takes and what it gives back.
  • Test each function with inputs whose answers you already know, before you connect them.
  • / always produces a float. Code that expects whole numbers should round or convert first.
  • One validation function with parameters for the limits replaces a pile of nearly identical loops.
  • A traceback through a function shows the call on one line and the failing line inside the function below it.

#Make it yours

  • Miles too. Add a function km_to_miles(km) (1 mile is 1.609344 km) and print the pace per mile as well.
  • Goal mode. Ask for a goal time instead, and print the pace needed to hit it.
  • Split table. For a 5K, print the expected time at each kilometre: 1 km, 2 km, up to 5 km.
  • Add the marathon. Make it option 4 at 42.195 km. Which functions need to change? (That's the point of small functions: only two of them do.)

#Further reading

  • Python docs: round() (opens in a new tab): note that round(2.5) gives 2, because Python rounds halves to the nearest even number.
  • Python docs: Format Specification Mini-Language (opens in a new tab): what :02d, :.1f, and :, mean inside an f-string, and why d refuses floats.
  • Think Python, chapter 3: Functions (opens in a new tab): Allen Downey's free textbook explains functions, parameters, and stack diagrams, with exercises at the end.

m6-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Write functions that take parameters and return a result instead of printing it.
  • Test a function with several calls whose answers you know in advance.
  • Recognize and fix the two classic function bugs: printing instead of returning, and changing a variable from the wrong scope.
  • Build a bigger function out of a loop, and reuse one function inside another.

Every exercise here asks for a function, not a whole program. Test each one with the sample calls given, and compare your output line by line. If a result surprises you, start the debugger with Ctrl+F5 and press F7 (Step into) on the call to see the function's local variables.

#Warm-up: print or return?

Predict the three lines this prints, in order, before opening the solution.

Show solution

Each call prints its "checking" line while it runs, and only the returned values (6 and 8) are added. So you see both "checking" lines first, then 14.

#Exercise 1: Initials

Write initials(first, last) that returns a person's initials in capitals with dots.

Need a hint?

first[0] is the first character of a string, and .upper() capitalizes it. Join the pieces with + and return the result.

Show solution

The function returns a string, so the caller decides what to do with it: print it, store it, or put it on a name badge.

#Exercise 2: Is this username allowed?

A game allows usernames of 3 to 15 characters with no spaces. Write is_valid_username(name) that returns True or False.

Need a hint?

len(name) gives the length, and " " in name is True if there's a space anywhere. A comparison already is True or False, so you can return it directly without an if.

Show solution

3 <= len(name) <= 15 is a chained comparison: it means 3 <= len(name) and len(name) <= 15. Functions that return True or False read nicely in an if: if is_valid_username(name):.

#Exercise 3: Keep a value in range

Games keep health between 0 and 100 no matter what happens. Write clamp(value, low, high) that returns low if value is below it, high if it's above, and value otherwise.

Need a hint?

Use early returns: one if that returns low, one that returns high, and a final return value for everything else.

Show solution

You'll use exactly this function in the next module's game, to keep a pet's hunger and energy between 0 and 10.

#Exercise 4: The average that won't compare

This program should print Honor roll! because the average of the scores is above 85. Instead it prints a number and then crashes. Find the bug and fix it.

Need a hint?

Read the last line of the error. What type is on the left side of >? What does a function give back when it has no return?

Show solution

print showed 86.33… on the screen, but the function handed back None, and None > 85 makes no sense to Python. Changing print to return sends the number to the if.

#Exercise 5: Experience points that won't add up

This function is supposed to add experience points to a global total. It crashes the first time it's called.

Rewrite it so the function takes the current XP as a parameter and returns the new total, and the main code stores the result. It should print 50 and then 75.

Need a hint?

Because the function assigns to xp, Python treats xp as a local variable for the whole function, so xp + amount tries to read a local that doesn't exist yet. (Older versions of Python word this as "local variable 'xp' referenced before assignment.") Pass the value in with a parameter, return the new value, and assign it back with xp = gain_xp(xp, 50).

Show solution

Python does have a global keyword that lets a function change a global variable, but parameters and return values are easier to follow and test: you can read xp = gain_xp(xp, 50) and know exactly what changed.

#Exercise 6: A text progress bar

Write progress_bar(done, total, width=20) that returns a bar made of # and - characters plus a percentage. Then use a loop to print the bar for 0 to 5 tasks out of 5.

Need a hint?

The number of # characters is done / total * width, rounded to a whole number. The rest of the width is -. "#" * 8 makes eight # characters. Build the string with + and return it.

Show solution

The default width=20 covers the common case, and the last line shows a caller choosing a shorter bar with a keyword argument.

#Challenge: A secret-message cipher

The Caesar cipher shifts every letter a fixed number of places along the alphabet. With a shift of 3, a becomes d, b becomes e, and z wraps around to c. Write two functions:

  • encode(message, shift) returns the message with every letter shifted. Make everything lowercase, and leave spaces and punctuation alone.
  • decode(message, shift) turns it back. Write it in one line by calling encode.

Step through a tiny version first to see how one letter's position is found and shifted:

Need a hint?

Keep the alphabet in a string. ALPHABET.find(ch) gives a letter's position (0 for a), or -1 if ch isn't a letter. (position + shift) % 26 wraps past z back to the start. And decoding is just encoding with the shift going the other way.

Show solution

decode works because Python's % always gives a result from 0 to 25 here, even for negative numbers: (0 - 3) % 26 is 23, which is x. Reusing encode means there's only one loop to get right. Try sending a friend a message with shift 13; encoding it twice gives back the original, because 13 + 13 = 26.

m7-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Read a traceback from the bottom up to find what went wrong and where.
  • Recognize the most common error types and what usually causes each one.
  • Catch an error you expect with try and except, so bad input can't crash your program.
  • Follow a step-by-step debugging routine, and use lists and dictionaries to hold an app's data.

A friend is testing your treasure-hunt game. They type their name, and then, instead of a number, they type ten. The game dies with this wall of red text:

You read short error messages from the bottom up back in Module 1. This one is longer and mentions three different lines, but it's not a jumble; it's a precise report, called a traceback, and once you know the order to read it in, it usually tells you the fix in under a minute.

#Read a traceback from the bottom up

Start at the last line. It always has two parts: the error's type, then a message.

ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'ten'

In plain words: int() was given the text 'ten', which isn't a number it can convert. Already you know what happened.

Now move up one entry to find where. Each File ... line ... entry is one function call that was still running when the crash happened:

  1. line 3, in ask_steps: the crash itself, at return int(text).
  2. line 6, in walk: the line that called ask_steps().
  3. line 10, in <module>: the top level of the file (Python calls it <module>), which called walk(name).

"Most recent call last" means the entries are in the order the calls were made, so the newest one, where the crash happened, sits at the bottom. In a big program, some entries may point into code you didn't write, such as a library. Scan upward for the first entry in your file; that's usually where the fix belongs. In Thonny you'll see your real file path instead of main.py, and your Python version may format the ^^^ markers a little differently.

Step through the same program and watch the stack grow one frame at a time, then stop at the crash:

The bug isn't really in int(), which did its job by refusing nonsense. The bug is that ask_steps trusted the user. You'll fix that in a moment with try.

#The errors you'll meet most

Almost every error a beginner hits is one of these eight. Learn to recognize them and you're halfway to the fix.

Error What it means Usual cause
SyntaxError Python can't read the code at all missing :, unclosed quote or bracket
IndentationError the indentation doesn't match the structure body of an if, for, or def not indented
NameError that name doesn't exist (yet) typo, or using a variable before setting it
TypeError the operation doesn't work on that type "Gold: " + 12, a missing argument, None + 1
ValueError right type, but an unusable value int("ten")
IndexError that list position doesn't exist items[3] in a three-item list
KeyError that dictionary key doesn't exist player["Gold"] when the key is "gold"
ZeroDivisionError dividing by zero averaging an empty list

Two of them deserve a closer look because Python helps you more than you'd expect. A SyntaxError is caught before your program runs a single line, so it points at a spot in the code rather than a chain of calls:

And recent versions of Python (3.10 and newer) often guess what you meant when you mistype a name:

Did you mean: 'score'? is about as direct as an error message gets.

#Catch the errors you expect with try and except

Some errors aren't bugs in your logic; they're things users will do. You can't stop someone typing ten, but you can plan for it. Put the risky line inside try:, and put what to do instead inside except with the specific error type:

If int(text) succeeds, return hands the number back and the loop ends. If it raises a ValueError, Python skips to the except block, prints the hint, and the while True loop asks again. Unlike .isdigit(), this accepts negative numbers like -2 (a basement floor) because int() itself decides what counts.

⚠️ Watch out

Name the error you expect. A bare except: with no error type catches everything, including typos in your own code like a NameError. Your program stops crashing, but it also stops telling you about real bugs. Write except ValueError: (or whichever error you actually expect) so anything else still shows a traceback.

#Lists and dictionaries hold your app's data

Real apps keep track of many things: a backpack full of items, a player's stats, a list of high scores. Two of Python's built-in types handle almost all of it.

A list keeps items in order, and each item has a position number called an index, starting at 0:

Negative indexes count from the end, so backpack[-1] is always the last item, however long the list grows.

A dictionary (or dict) stores values under names called keys, written as key: value pairs inside curly brackets. You look values up by key instead of by position:

.items() gives you each key and value together, perfect for a for loop. .get("armor", 0) returns the value if the key exists, or the default 0 if it doesn't, without crashing.

Each type has its own signature error. Ask a three-item list for index 3 (there are only 0, 1, and 2):

Ask a dictionary for a key that isn't there, even one that differs only in capital letters:

A KeyError message is just the missing key. When you see one, compare it letter by letter with the keys you actually created.

#A debugging routine that works

When something breaks, don't start changing lines at random. Work through the same steps every time:

  • Reproduce it. Write down the exact input that caused the crash, so you can test your fix with it.
  • Check the values. Errors are almost always about a value that isn't what you assumed. Add a temporary print(f"{text=}") just before the failing line (the = prints the name and the value, like text='ten'), or run the debugger with Ctrl+F5, step to the line, and read the Variables panel.
  • Change one thing at a time. If you change three lines and it works, you won't know which change mattered, or whether the other two broke something else.

Not every bug crashes. A logic error runs fine and gives the wrong answer, like a score that never goes up. There's no traceback to read, so the "check the values" step does all the work: step through the code and watch for the moment a variable stops matching what you expected.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A traceback ends with IndexError: list index out of range. Where do you look first?

  • That's the outermost call, usually far from the problem.

  • The bottom entries show where the crash happened; check which index was used and how long the list really is.

  • An IndexError is about list positions, not input.

Show answer

B. The bottom entries show where the crash happened; check which index was used and how long the list really is.

2Which error does int("3.5") raise?

  • It's a string (the right type for int()), but its value can't be read as a whole number.

  • int() accepts strings, so the type is fine; the problem is the value.

  • The code is valid Python; the problem only appears when it runs.

Show answer

A. It's a string (the right type for int()), but its value can't be read as a whole number.

3stats = {"hp": 7}. What does stats.get("mp", 0) give?

  • That's what stats["mp"] would do. .get() exists to avoid it.

  • The key "mp" doesn't exist, so .get() returns the default you gave it.

  • 7 belongs to the key "hp", not "mp".

Show answer

B. The key "mp" doesn't exist, so .get() returns the default you gave it.

4Why is except ValueError: better than a bare except: around int(text)?

  • Speed isn't the reason.

  • It's valid Python, just risky.

  • A bare except: would also hide a typo like NameError, leaving you with a program that fails silently.

Show answer

C. A bare except: would also hide a typo like NameError, leaving you with a program that fails silently.

Key takeaways

  • Read a traceback bottom-up: the last line says what happened, the File entries above it say where, newest call last.
  • SyntaxError and IndentationError stop the program before it starts; the others happen while it runs.
  • Wrap risky lines in try and catch the specific error you expect, like except ValueError:.
  • Lists hold items in order by index (starting at 0); dictionaries hold values by key. IndexError and KeyError mean the position or key doesn't exist.
  • Debug by reproducing, reading, checking values, and changing one thing at a time.

#Further reading

  • Python tutorial: Errors and Exceptions (opens in a new tab): the official guide to tracebacks, try, and except, with short examples.
  • Python docs: Built-in Exceptions (opens in a new tab): a description of every error type, for when you meet one that isn't in the table above.
  • Python tutorial: Dictionaries (opens in a new tab): creating, updating, and looping over dictionaries, plus list methods higher up the same page.

What you'll learn

  • Store an app's state in a dictionary and pass it to functions that update it.
  • Explain why a function can change a dictionary it's given, but not a number.
  • Build a validated menu loop that calls a different function for each choice.
  • Read a KeyError traceback and fix the typo behind it.

Time to put loops, functions, validation, and dictionaries together into one complete program: a virtual pet. Each turn you choose to feed, play, or rest. Every turn the pet gets hungrier and a little more bored. Keep it fed and happy for eight turns and it grows up; let hunger hit 10 or fun hit 0 and the game ends. Here's a short game that goes badly:

Here's the plan. The main loop is the boss: it shows the stats, gets a valid choice, hands the pet to the right function, then lets time pass and checks the rules.

Save a new Thonny file as pet.py in your m7 folder and build it in six steps.

#Step 1: The pet is a dictionary

The pet has a name and four numbers that change. You could use five separate variables, but then every function would need five parameters. A dictionary keeps them together under one name, so you can pass the whole pet around as a single value.

Inside the f-string, the keys use single quotes (pet['name']) because the f-string itself uses double quotes. Mixing them up ends the string early and gives a SyntaxError. (Python 3.12 and newer allow matching quotes there, but older versions, which you may have in Thonny, don't, so single quotes are the safe habit.)

#Step 2: Actions that change the pet

Each action is a function that takes the pet and updates some of its values. A clamp helper keeps every stat between 0 and 10, the same idea as Exercise 3 in the last practice lesson.

The third play is refused: after two games energy is 0, and the bare return leaves the function early, before any stats change. That's an early return with no value, used purely to stop.

Now, something should be bothering you. In Module 6, collect(coins) changed its own copy of coins and the outside value stayed at 10. Yet here feed(pet) really does change the pet. Step through and compare:

The difference is what the line inside the function does. coins = coins + 5 makes the local name point to a brand-new number; the global name is untouched. pet["hunger"] = ... doesn't make a new dictionary. It reaches into the one dictionary that both names refer to and changes a value inside it. So the change is visible everywhere. Lists behave the same way: backpack.append("map") inside a function changes the caller's list.

#Step 3: A KeyError to read

While typing feed, it's easy to write hungry instead of hunger. Here's what that looks like:

Bottom up, as always. KeyError: 'hungry': some dictionary was asked for the key 'hungry' and doesn't have it. One entry up: line 3, inside feed. Compare that line with the dictionary on line 7 and the typo jumps out. Change pet["hungry"] to pet["hunger"] and run again.

💡 Tip

Dictionary keys are just strings, so Python can't warn you about a misspelled key until that line runs. Copy and paste key names from the line that creates the dictionary, or keep the full list of keys in a comment above it.

#Step 4: The menu loop

The player chooses by typing a word. ask_choice keeps asking until the word is on the menu, then returns it. The main loop uses if/elif to call the matching function, and break ends the game on quit.

The return inside while True does double duty: it hands back the choice and ends the loop, because a function stops the moment it returns. That's why ask_choice doesn't need a break.

#Step 5: Time passes, and the game can end

After each action, a turn goes by. pass_time makes the pet hungrier, a little more bored, and one turn older. trouble checks the losing rules and returns a reason as a string, or an empty string if all is well. Keeping the rules in their own function means the main loop doesn't need to know the details.

This test lets time pass with no care at all, to see how long a neglected pet lasts. Three turns. That's a useful number when you balance the game: if neglect ended things after 20 turns, the game would be too easy.

#Step 6: Count the actions and assemble everything

One more dictionary keeps a tally of how often the player chose each action. counts[choice] = counts[choice] + 1 works because the menu words are exactly the dictionary's keys. Here's the whole game, played to a win:

Look at how short the main loop is. Each line names a job, and the details live in functions you've already tested. If the pet gets hungry too fast, you change one number in pass_time; if you want a new action, you write one function and add one elif. That's what "assembling an application" means: small, tested parts, connected by a simple loop.

Before calling it finished, play it like someone trying to break it: press Enter at the name prompt, type FEED in capitals, type rest with spaces, and spam play until the pet is too tired. Each case should be handled without a traceback.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does feed(pet) change the pet in the main program, when collect(coins) in Module 6 didn't change coins?

  • Both are ordinary values; neither is automatically global.

  • Both names refer to the same dictionary, so a change inside it shows up everywhere. Reassigning a name never affects the caller.

  • Docstrings are documentation; they don't change how the code runs.

Show answer

B. Both names refer to the same dictionary, so a change inside it shows up everywhere. Reassigning a name never affects the caller.

2Why does trouble(pet) return a string like "too hungry" instead of printing the message itself?

  • Returning a value keeps the rules separate from the screen output, and makes trouble easy to test.

  • Functions can print; feed does. It's a design choice.

  • print never ends a loop.

Show answer

A. Returning a value keeps the rules separate from the screen output, and makes trouble easy to test.

3A player types Rest with a capital R. What happens?

  • That would happen without .lower().

  • Cleaning up input before validating it lets small differences through without bothering the player.

  • The choice is cleaned up and validated before it's ever used as a key in counts.

Show answer

B. Cleaning up input before validating it lets small differences through without bothering the player.

Key takeaways

  • A dictionary keeps an app's related values together, so one parameter can carry the whole state.
  • Changing a value inside a dictionary or list is visible to every name that refers to it; reassigning a name is not.
  • A menu function that validates and returns the choice keeps the main loop short.
  • Put game rules in functions that return answers, and keep the main loop in charge of what happens next.
  • A KeyError names the missing key; compare it with the keys you created.

#Make it yours

  • Random events. import random, and in pass_time give a 1-in-5 chance (random.randint(1, 5) == 1) that the pet finds a toy and gains 2 fun.
  • A new action. Add bathe, with a clean stat that drops each turn. You'll need one new function, one new key, one elif, and one menu word.
  • Two pets. Keep a list of two pet dictionaries and ask which one to care for each turn.
  • Moods. Write mood(pet) that returns "happy", "grumpy", or "sleepy" from the stats, and show it in show_status.

#Further reading

  • Python tutorial: Data Structures (opens in a new tab): lists, dictionaries, and how to loop over them, from the people who make Python.
  • Python docs: Mapping types (dict) (opens in a new tab): every dictionary method, including get, items, and keys.
