m7-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Read a traceback to find the error type, the failing line, and the value that caused it.
  • Fix NameError, TypeError, IndexError, and logic bugs that produce no error at all.
  • Use try and except ValueError to validate decimal input.
  • Use dictionaries to look up prices, count things, and keep records up to date.

Half of these exercises hand you broken code. Resist the urge to rewrite it from scratch; the skill you're practicing is finding the one thing that's wrong. Read the error first, form a guess, and test the guess. When there's no error message, use print(f"{name=}") or Thonny's debugger to check values.

#Warm-up: read before you fix

This checkout program crashes. Without changing anything, answer three questions: What type of error is it? On which line and in which function does it happen? Which value in the data is the real culprit?

Show solution
  • Type: TypeError, because / was used with a string and a number.
  • Where: line 2, in price_with_discount. It was called from line 7 in checkout, which was called from line 11.
  • Culprit: the second item's discount is "5", a string, not the number 5.

Here's the sneaky part: 15 * "5" doesn't crash. Multiplying a string by a whole number repeats it, so Python made "555555555555555" and only failed one step later, at / 100. The fix is in the data: change "5" to 5. The crash line and the cause are often a few steps apart, which is why you check the values on the failing line, not just the line itself.

#Exercise 1: A birthday card with two bugs

This program has two bugs. Fix the first, run it, read the next error, and fix that too.

When it works, it should print:

Need a hint?

The first error names the exact word Python doesn't recognize; compare it, letter by letter, with the variables the program creates. After that, remember what type input() returns. Can you add 1 to a string? And can you join a number onto a string with +?

Show solution

Bug 1 was the typo nmae (a NameError). Bug 2 was a TypeError: age was the string "14", so age + 1 can't work. Converting with int() fixes the math, and the f-string handles turning the number back into text.

#Exercise 2: Ask for a price

Write ask_price(prompt) that keeps asking until the user types a number of zero or more, then returns it as a float. Decimals like 4.50 must work.

Need a hint?

.isdigit() won't work here because of the decimal point. Use try: with float(text) and except ValueError:. Inside a while True loop, continue sends you back for another try, and return ends everything once the price is good.

Show solution

There are two kinds of bad input, so there are two checks: except handles text that isn't a number at all, and the if handles numbers that are the wrong size.

#Exercise 3: The podium is off by one

This should print the top three finishers as 1 Mia, 2 Theo, 3 Ana. It prints the wrong names, then crashes.

Need a hint?

People count places from 1. Lists count positions from 0. Which list index holds the first-place finisher?

Show solution

finishers[place - 1] turns place 1 into index 0. (Python also has enumerate(finishers, start=1), which gives you the number and the item together, but the subtraction makes the off-by-one visible.)

#Exercise 4: The snack shop

Use this price list. Keep asking for items until the customer types done. Add each known item to the total; for anything else, print a polite message instead of crashing. Then print the total.

Need a hint?

prices["cookie"] would raise a KeyError. Check first with if item in prices:, which is True only when the key exists.

Show solution

.lower() lets Chips match the key "chips". Adding a new snack to the shop is now a one-word change to the dictionary; none of the loop needs to change.

#Exercise 5: The high score that's too low

No crash, no traceback, just a wrong answer. The scores entered are 9, 10, and 7, but the program says the high score is 9.

Step through a shorter run and watch best refuse to change when 10 arrives:

Need a hint?

Look at the quotes around the values in the trace. How does Python compare two strings? It goes character by character, like a dictionary does with words. Which comes first, "1" or "9"?

Show solution

As strings, "10" is "less than" "9", because the first characters are compared first and "1" comes before "9". Converting to int compares the numbers instead. This is the most dangerous kind of bug: it doesn't crash, so you only catch it if you test with an input whose answer you already know.

#Exercise 6: Count the words

Count how many times each word appears in a sentence, print every count, then print the most common word.

Need a hint?

sentence.split() turns the sentence into a list of words. Start with an empty dictionary, counts = {}. For each word, counts.get(word, 0) + 1 gives the new count whether or not the word has been seen before. Find the most common with a best-so-far loop over counts.items().

Show solution

Dictionaries remember the order keys were added, which is why the words print in the order they first appear. The .get(word, 0) trick is the standard way to count with a dictionary.

#Challenge: An arcade high-score table

Build a small command-driven app that keeps each player's best score in a dictionary. It understands four commands:

  • add NAME SCORE records a score, but only replaces a player's entry if the new score is higher.
  • show lists every player and their best score.
  • best names the top player.
  • quit ends the program.

Anything else, a missing part, or a score that isn't a whole number should get a helpful message, never a traceback.

Need a hint?

command.split() turns "add Ana 1200" into ["add", "Ana", "1200"]. Check len(parts) before using parts[1] or parts[2], or you'll hit an IndexError. Put int(parts[2]) inside try. Write a function for each command, such as add_score(scores, name, points), and keep the main loop to choosing which one to call.

Show solution

The order of checks in the add branch matters: count the parts before reading parts[2], and convert inside try before calling add_score. By the time add_score runs, its inputs are guaranteed to be clean, so the function itself stays simple. That "check at the door" design is exactly what your capstone will need.

m8-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • List the eight things your capstone app must do, and which module taught each one.
  • Choose a project that's big enough to show your skills and small enough to finish.
  • Write a sample session that shows, line by line, what the user will see.
  • Plan your app's data and name its functions, with what each takes and gives back.

The virtual pet from Module 7 is under 100 lines. It asks questions, validates every answer, keeps its state in a dictionary, runs a main loop, splits its work into small functions, and ends cleanly. That one program checks every box on the capstone list below, which means you already know enough to build an app of your own. The difference this time is that nobody hands you the design. You decide what to build and how to break it up, and that's the skill this module is about.

#The brief

Build a complete text-based Python application that someone else could sit down and use without your help. It must have all eight of these:

# Requirement What it looks like in your app Learned in
1 Input and output asks the user questions and prints clear, readable results Module 3
2 Variables and data keeps track of its state, using at least one list or dictionary Modules 2 and 7
3 Decisions if/elif/else changes what happens based on the user or the data Module 4
4 Loops a main loop that keeps the app running, plus at least one other loop Module 5
5 Functions at least four of your own, each with a docstring, most of them returning a value Module 6
6 Validation every question re-asks politely when the answer doesn't make sense Modules 5 and 6
7 Error handling no input can crash it; try/except wherever text becomes a number Module 7
8 A clean exit the user can quit at any point, and the app ends with a summary Module 5

You'll hand in four things: your .py file, a test table showing what you tried (built in the last lesson), a short README explaining how to use the app, and a two-minute demo.

#Pick a project

Choose something you'd actually want to use or play; you'll spend hours with it. Here are six ideas, from most approachable to most ambitious. Each one can meet all eight requirements.

Project Level What it stores The tricky part
Unit converter toolkit: a menu of at least three conversions (cooking cups to millilitres, km to miles, and so on) Starter a list of every conversion done, shown at the end validating decimal input with try/except
Flashcard trainer: quiz yourself on vocabulary, then re-ask the ones you missed Starter a dictionary of term to answer, a list of misses comparing answers fairly (spaces, capitals)
Word guessing game: guess a secret word one letter at a time with limited lives Medium the secret word, a list of guessed letters, lives left showing _ a _ _ e with a loop, and rejecting repeat guesses
Budget tracker: log spending by category and see where the money went Medium a dictionary of category to total the report: biggest category and percentages
Text adventure: explore rooms, collect items, solve one puzzle to escape Stretch a dictionary of rooms, a list for the inventory rooms that link to each other with exits
Turn-based battle: fight a series of monsters, choosing attack, defend, or heal each turn Stretch dictionaries for the player and each monster balancing the numbers so it's winnable but not easy

The next lesson builds a small text adventure as a worked example. If you choose that idea, make your map, items, and puzzle your own rather than extending the example.

💡 Tip

Your own idea is welcome, as long as it ticks all eight boxes. A quick test: can you describe the smallest working version in three sentences? If not, shrink it until you can. You can always add features after it works.

#Write the sample session first

Before any code, write out what the screen will show from start to finish, including your user making mistakes. This forces you to decide how the app actually behaves, and it doubles as your first test later. Here's one for the budget tracker:

Notice how much design is hiding in there. Categories are a fixed list. Amounts reject the $ sign. The report shows percentages. Quitting prints a summary. Every one of those is a decision you'd otherwise make halfway through coding, usually badly.

#Plan the data and the functions

Next, decide what your app has to remember and which functions will do the work. Most text apps share the same overall shape:

For the budget tracker, the data is a dictionary like {"food": 12.5, "fun": 20.0} plus a count of expenses. The functions might be:

Function Takes Gives back
ask_choice(prompt, options) a question and a list of allowed answers one of the allowed answers
ask_amount(prompt) a question a float of 0 or more
add_expense(totals, category, amount) the dictionary, a category, an amount nothing; it updates the dictionary
biggest_category(totals) the dictionary the name of the biggest category
show_report(totals) the dictionary nothing; it prints the report

Naming the functions now pays off twice. You can write and test each one alone, as you did with the pace calculator. And when you get stuck, you'll know exactly which small piece isn't working.

#Your planning template

Copy this into a file called plan.txt next to your project (or into a comment at the top of your .py file) and fill in every line before you start coding.

#Planning mistakes that cost the most time

⚠️ Watch out

Starting with the hardest feature. If the exciting part is a boss battle, it's tempting to code that first. But without a working menu loop around it, you can't test it. Build the boring skeleton first; the next lesson shows you how.

⚠️ Watch out

A plan with no "how do I quit?" Apps built without an exit in mind end up with while True loops that can only be stopped with Thonny's Stop button. Decide now: a quit command, a menu number, or a game-over condition, and write it into your sample session.

⚠️ Watch out

Ten separate variables for one thing. If you catch yourself planning player_name, player_hp, player_gold, and player_level, that's a dictionary: player = {"name": ..., "hp": ..., ...}. One name to pass around, and one place to add new fields.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Which is the best first goal for a flashcard trainer?

  • Those are good stretch goals, but nothing can be tested until the basic loop works.

  • This is small enough to finish today, and every later feature builds on it.

  • Content can be added any time; start with three cards and working code.

Show answer

B. This is small enough to finish today, and every later feature builds on it.

2Your plan has ask_amount(prompt) returning a float. Why plan the return type now?

  • A clear promise about what comes back is what lets you build the rest of the app on top of it.

  • Python decides types while the program runs; the plan is for you.

  • Nothing requires floats; what matters is knowing what each function gives back.

Show answer

A. A clear promise about what comes back is what lets you build the rest of the app on top of it.

3Why write a sample session that includes the user making mistakes?

  • Length isn't the goal.

  • If the sample shows Amount: $12 getting a polite hint, you know to write that validation and you know how to test it.

  • It does the opposite: it lists exactly which validation you need.

Show answer

B. If the sample shows Amount: $12 getting a polite hint, you know to write that validation and you know how to test it.

Key takeaways

  • The capstone needs input, data, decisions, loops, functions, validation, error handling, and a clean exit.
  • Pick a project you care about, then shrink it to a smallest version you can describe in three sentences.
  • A sample session, mistakes included, is both your design and your first test.
  • Plan your data and your function names (with what each takes and gives back) before writing code.

#Further reading

  • Invent Your Own Computer Games with Python (opens in a new tab): a free online book by Al Sweigart full of complete text games. Chapter 7, "Designing Hangman with Flowcharts", plans a whole game before writing code, the same way this lesson does.
  • Python docs: the random module (opens in a new tab): random.choice() and random.randint() are all most games need.

m8-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Start your capstone from a skeleton that already runs, validates input, and quits cleanly.
  • Build in milestones, each one small enough to finish and test in a single session.
  • Follow a complete worked example, an escape-room text adventure, from skeleton to finished game.
  • Diagnose the problems that most often stall a capstone.

The biggest risk in a capstone isn't a hard bug. It's spending three sessions writing 200 lines without running them, then facing 15 errors at once. The fix is to build in milestones: small steps that each end with a program that runs. If a milestone breaks something, you only have a few new lines to suspect.

#The starter skeleton

Copy this into Thonny and save it in your m8 folder under your project's name. It runs right now: it has a menu loop, a choice validator, a number validator with try/except, one placeholder feature, and a summary at the end. Your job is to replace the placeholders, one milestone at a time.

Two new things are worth a sentence each:

  • ", ".join(options) glues the items of a list into one string, with ", " between them, so the hint reads a, q.
  • The whole main program lives inside a function called main(), and the very last line calls it. That keeps the app's variables local (so every other function has to receive them as parameters, the habit from Module 6), and it means return inside main() ends the program cleanly from anywhere.

⚠️ Watch out

If your program runs and nothing at all happens, check the last line. Without the call main(), Python reads every def and then stops, because nothing ever calls them.

#The five milestones

Work through these in order. Don't start a milestone until the previous one runs and you've tested it.

Milestone Goal Done when
M1: Skeleton Rename the skeleton's menu and placeholders for your app. It starts, shows your menu, rejects nonsense, and quits with a summary.
M2: Core, once Make your single most important feature work one time. You can do the main thing (one quiz question, one conversion, one move) correctly.
M3: Data and repetition Store results in your list or dictionary and let the loop repeat the feature. Several rounds work in a row, and the data remembers them.
M4: Bulletproof input Validate every input and add try/except wherever text becomes a number. Nothing you type can produce a traceback.
M5: Finish and polish Add the win, lose, or end conditions, the final summary, and tidy messages. A friend can use it without asking you anything.

After each milestone, save a copy (capstone_m2.py, capstone_m3.py, ...) so you can always get back to the last version that worked.

#Worked example: Escape the Lab

Here's a small text adventure built through the same five milestones. You wake up in a dark lab. To escape you need to find a flashlight, use it to read a note with the door code, and type the code into a keypad. Back in Module 2, The Lantern Cave tracked a hero's stats but couldn't respond to the player; this adventure listens to every command. It's about 140 lines when finished.

#M1: Skeleton

Commands are typed as words, like go north, so the first job is splitting the player's text into a verb and a noun. split_command always returns exactly two words (using "" when one is missing), which means the main loop never has to worry about an IndexError.

Notice that QUIT with spaces and capitals still quits. Every later command gets that for free, because the cleanup happens in one place.

#M2: Core, once

The core of an adventure is moving between rooms. Each room is a dictionary with a description and its exits, and all the rooms live in one big dictionary keyed by name. move looks up the exits for the current room and returns where the player ends up, which is the same room if the direction isn't allowed.

Step through a two-room version. Watch here stay the same after the bad direction, then change after the good one:

rooms[here]["exits"] reads in two steps: rooms[here] gets the current room's dictionary, and ["exits"] gets the exits inside it. A dictionary inside a dictionary sounds complicated, but each step is a lookup you already know.

#M3: Data and repetition

Now the player can pick things up. The inventory is a list; each room's "item" is a string, set to "" once it's taken so it can't be taken twice. A tiny helper, can_see, holds the darkness rule so that both describe and take can use it:

take changes both the inventory list and the room's dictionary, and both changes stick because it's changing values inside them, just like feed(pet) in Module 7.

#M4: Bulletproof input

The keypad is the one place where text becomes a number, so that's where try/except goes. ask_code loops until it gets a whole number, and move compares it with the code:

Then the test list for this milestone: go with no direction, go up, GO NORTH, an empty line, four at the keypad, and a wrong code. In the finished game, each of those gets a message instead of a traceback. (go alone hits the direction == "" check in move; an empty line falls through to "I don't understand that.")

#M5: Finish and polish

The last milestone adds the ending: the loop runs while here != "outside", a moves counter goes up on every successful move, and a final message reports the count. It also adds the look and inventory commands, a description when you enter each room, and a docstring on every function. Here's the finished game, played from start to escape, including a few mistakes:

Check it against the brief: input and output everywhere; a dictionary of rooms and an inventory list; decisions in every function; a main loop plus the keypad loop; nine functions with docstrings; validated commands; try/except at the keypad; and quit or escape both end the game with a message. make_rooms() builds a fresh map each time it's called, so adding a "play again?" question at the end would be a short change.

#When you get stuck

What you see Likely cause What to try
The program runs and does nothing No main() call on the last line Add it, unindented
The same message prints forever without waiting input() isn't inside the loop Move the input() line into the loop body
The loop never ends Nothing in the loop makes the condition False Check that break, return, or a changing variable is actually reached
A function's result is None One path through the function has no return Step into it with F7 and see which path it took
A change to your data doesn't stick You reassigned a name inside a function instead of changing a key Return the new value, or change data["key"] directly
It works for you but crashes for a friend They typed something you didn't test Read the traceback, then add their input to your test table

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does split_command always return exactly two words, even for an empty line?

  • Lists can have any length.

  • Handling the odd cases once, inside one function, keeps every caller simple and safe.

  • It's about safety, not difficulty.

Show answer

B. Handling the odd cases once, inside one function, keeps every caller simple and safe.

2move returns the same room when the direction is blocked. How does main use that?

  • The return value carries the answer, so main decides what a successful move means.

  • here is a string in main; move can't change it, which is why it returns the result.

  • Blocked moves just print a message and return the current room.

Show answer

A. The return value carries the answer, so main decides what a successful move means.

3You're at M3 and adding a feature breaks M2, which worked an hour ago. What's the fastest way back?

  • That throws away all your working code.

  • Saving a copy after each milestone gives you a known-good version, and the bug is in the difference.

  • That hides the error instead of fixing it.

Show answer

B. Saving a copy after each milestone gives you a known-good version, and the bug is in the difference.

Key takeaways

  • Start from a skeleton that runs, and keep it running after every milestone.
  • Build the core feature once before adding repetition, data, and validation around it.
  • Handle messy input in one place (like split_command or ask_code) so the rest of the program can trust it.
  • Keep main() in charge, pass data to functions as parameters, and use return values to report what happened.
  • Save a copy after each milestone so you always have a version that works.

#Further reading

  • Python docs: str.join() (opens in a new tab): how join works, and why it's called on the separator rather than the list.
  • Python docs: __main__, the top-level code environment (opens in a new tab): explains the if __name__ == "__main__": line you'll see at the bottom of other people's programs, often just above a call to main().

m8-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Write a test table that covers normal, edge, and deliberately bad inputs.
  • Check your functions automatically with a small check helper and with assert.
  • Polish your code and messages so a stranger can use and read your app.
  • Write a README, give a two-minute demo, and judge your work against the rubric.

Your app works when you use it. Unfortunately, that's the weakest test there is, because you know exactly what it expects. Hand it to a friend and within a minute they'll press Enter on an empty line, type TWELVE, or answer a yes-or-no question with maybe. This lesson is about finding those cracks before anyone else does, then presenting the result.

#Step 1: Build a test table

A test table lists what you'll type, what should happen, and what did happen. Fill in the "should happen" column before you run anything, or you'll be tempted to decide the program's behavior was correct after seeing it. Cover each of these kinds of input:

  • Normal: the things a user is supposed to type.
  • Empty: just pressing Enter.
  • Wrong type: a word where a number belongs, or a number where a word belongs.
  • Messy formatting: capitals, extra spaces, $ signs.
  • Boundaries: the smallest and largest allowed values, and one step past each.
  • Order and repetition: doing something twice, or out of order.
  • Leaving early: quitting at the first prompt, in the middle, and at the end.

Here are the first rows for Escape the Lab from the last lesson:

# Kind What I typed What should happen What happened Pass?
1 Normal go north in the lab move to the hall and describe it as expected yes
2 Empty Enter "I don't understand that." as expected yes
3 Messy GO North same as go north as expected yes
4 Missing part go "Go where? Try: go north" as expected yes
5 Wrong type four at the keypad digits hint, then ask again as expected yes
6 Repetition take twice in the storeroom the second time: "nothing here to take" as expected yes
7 Boundary 99999999999 at the keypad "Wrong code" as expected yes
8 Leaving early quit as the first command a goodbye message, no traceback as expected yes

Aim for at least 12 rows, and make sure every input() in your program appears somewhere in the table. When a row fails, don't just fix it: keep the row, so you can check later changes haven't broken it again.

#Step 2: Let Python check your functions

Functions that take values and return a result can be tested automatically, which is much faster than typing the same inputs over and over. A tiny helper prints PASS or FAIL for each check. Here it's testing an early version of split_command, before the .strip().lower() cleanup was added:

One failure, and the output says exactly what went wrong. split(" ") splits at every single space, so leading spaces produce empty strings. (The "empty line" test passed by luck, which is worth knowing too.) Switching to text.strip().lower().split(), which splits on any run of spaces and ignores spaces at the ends, makes all five pass. Keep test_lab.py next to your project and run it after every change.

Python also has a built-in one-line check, assert. It does nothing if the condition is True and stops the program with an AssertionError if it's False:

The third check failed. But look closer: 2 out of 3 is 66.7%, which rounds to 67. The test was wrong, not the code. When a test fails, ask which one is mistaken before you change anything.

#Step 3: Throw nasty input at your validators

Your validation functions are the front door of your app, so test them hardest. The input= trick you've seen all course works for this too: feed a list of strange answers and watch what gets through.

Two surprises. float() understands 1e3 (scientific notation for 1000) and even nan ("not a number"). Here the range check happens to reject both, but if your range went up to 5000, 1e3 would sail through as 1000. That's not necessarily a bug, but now you know, and you can decide. Tests that teach you something about your own code are the most valuable kind.

#Step 4: Polish

Polish is what makes an app feel finished. Work down this list with your code open:

  • Names. Every variable and function name says what it holds or does. Rename x, thing, and data2.
  • Docstrings. Every function has one. If a function is longer than about 25 lines, it's probably doing two jobs; split it.
  • Constants. Fixed numbers and settings live at the top in capitals (DOOR_CODE, ROUNDS), not scattered through the code.
  • Comments. Explain why, not what. # 21.0975 km is a half marathon helps; # set x to 5 doesn't.
  • Messages. Every hint tells the user what to type instead. Spelling and punctuation are consistent.
  • Leftovers. Delete debugging print lines and commented-out experiments.
  • Fresh start. Press Stop (or Ctrl+F2) to restart Thonny's Shell, then run with F5. This catches code that only worked because of a variable left over from an earlier run.

Here's the kind of change polish makes:

#Step 5: Write a README

A README is a short text file that tells someone what your app is and how to use it. Save this as README.txt next to your .py file and fill it in:

#Step 6: Present it in two minutes

A good demo has a plan. Practice it once out loud with a timer.

Time What to show
0:00–0:15 What the app is and who it's for, in one or two sentences
0:15–1:00 A normal run of the main feature
1:00–1:30 Try to break it live: empty input, a word instead of a number, quitting early
1:30–2:00 One piece of code you're proud of, and one bug you fixed

The "try to break it" part impresses people far more than a perfect run, because it shows you thought about real users.

#The rubric

Score yourself honestly before you hand in. Each row is worth up to 4 points, for 24 in total.

Criterion 4: Excellent 3: Good 2: Developing 1: Beginning
It works Runs start to finish; no test input causes a traceback Runs; one rare input crashes Main feature works, but other parts crash Doesn't run, or the main feature is missing
Requirements All eight from the brief, each used where it makes sense Seven of eight Five or six Four or fewer
Validation and errors Every input is validated, with try/except wherever text becomes a number, and every hint is helpful Most inputs validated; hints are clear Some inputs validated Little or no validation
Code organization At least four functions with docstrings and return values; short main loop; clear names and constants Functions used well, a few long or unclear spots Some functions, but most code is in one block One long block of code
Testing A test table of 12+ rows covering every kind of input, plus automatic checks 8 to 11 rows, most kinds covered A few rows No test evidence
Communication Complete README; clear two-minute demo that explains a bug fix README and demo with small gaps README or demo missing parts Neither

#Look back

Write a few sentences for each of these. They're for you, but they also make a great final paragraph for your README.

  • What was the hardest bug, and what finally helped you find it: the traceback, a print, the debugger, or a test?
  • Which of your functions could you reuse in a different program without changing it?
  • What would you plan differently if you started again tomorrow?
  • Which milestone saved you from a bigger problem later?

#What to learn next

You can now write complete programs that take input, make decisions, repeat work, recover from bad input, and organize themselves into functions. Here's where those skills lead:

  • Save data between runs. Right now your high scores and budgets vanish when the program ends. Files fix that: open(), write(), and read() are a short step from what you know.
  • Draw with code. The turtle module comes with Python and turns loops and functions into drawings and simple games.
  • Make real games. Pygame Zero lets you write arcade-style games in plain Python. Install the pgzero package with Thonny's Tools › Manage packages..., then switch on Run › Pygame Zero mode.
  • Model bigger things. When your dictionaries start needing their own functions, you're ready for classes, Python's way of bundling data and the functions that work on it.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why fill in the "what should happen" column before running your tests?

  • Once you've seen the output, it's easy to convince yourself it was correct all along.

  • Thonny doesn't read your test table; it's for you.

  • It's about honest results, not speed.

Show answer

A. Once you've seen the output, it's easy to convince yourself it was correct all along.

2assert percent(2, 3) == 66 fails with an AssertionError. What should you do first?

  • That could break a function that was right all along.

  • 2 out of 3 is 66.7%, which rounds to 67, so here the test needs fixing.

  • A failing test is information; deleting it throws that away.

Show answer

B. 2 out of 3 is 66.7%, which rounds to 67, so here the test needs fixing.

3Which test row is most likely to find a crash in a validated menu?

  • That's the case you've already tried a dozen times.

  • Empty and messy input are the cases beginners most often forget to handle.

  • Running it again repeats the same behavior unless the inputs change.

Show answer

B. Empty and messy input are the cases beginners most often forget to handle.

Key takeaways

  • Test with normal, empty, wrong-type, messy, boundary, repeated, and early-exit inputs, and write the expected result first.
  • Automatic checks (check helpers or assert) make retesting your functions instant.
  • When a test fails, decide whether the code or the test is wrong before changing anything.
  • Polish names, docstrings, constants, comments, and messages so a stranger can use and read your app.
  • A README and a short demo that includes breaking the app on purpose show what you built and how well you built it.

#Further reading

  • Python tutorial: Reading and Writing Files (opens in a new tab): the next step for saving high scores or budgets between runs.
  • Python docs: turtle graphics (opens in a new tab): drawing with Python, built in and ready to use in Thonny.
  • Pygame Zero documentation (opens in a new tab): an introduction and tutorials for writing games with very little setup code.
